plaintext;"></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Both the machines exchange the SSH versions and negotiate crypto algorithms, and each side runs a key exchange protocol. The SSH server sends the public key and a signature, which the client machine verifies. That host key is then checked against the known_hosts file.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Both the machines then derive session keys on their end and do not share them over the network. Same keys, computed separately, never put on the wire. Then the SSH client starts authentication by sending the public key for login. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The SSH server matches the public key in the authorized_keys, and the SSH client also signs the auth request with the private key and sends the digital signature to the SSH server.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The private key never leaves your machine. The server will verify the signature with the client public key. This completes the SSH authentication, and now the session is open for communication.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Top 6 Techniques to Make Your AI System Efficient</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Serving LLMs at scale is expensive. plaintext;">It uses an LLM to select an action, executes that action, evaluates the result, and repeats the process until the task is complete. Let’s take a closer look at each of these components:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Brain: The LLM is the core. It reads the situation, thinks, and decides what to do next. The big shift from chatbot to agent: the model isn’t writing text anymore, it’s making choices.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><span>Planning: Hard tasks need more than one step. Agents break them down using methods like Chain of Thought (think step by step), Tree of Thoughts (try options, pick the best), or</span><br><span>Reflexion (learn from mistakes and retry). Planning turns a fuzzy goal into clear actions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Tools: An LLM without tools is a brain in a jar. Tools are functions the model can call, like web search, code execution, APIs, files, or browsers (often using the MCP standard). The model requests a tool, the system runs it, and the result comes back.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Memory: Without memory, every turn starts from zero. Short-term memory is the context window. Long-term memory lives in vector stores, files, and knowledge bases. When the window fills up, agents summarize old turns and carry the summary forward.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Loop: All four pieces work together in a cycle. The agent looks at the current state, decides what to do, uses a tool, sees the result, and repeats. It keeps going until it gives a final answer.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Guardrails: Not strictly anatomy, but important. Sandboxing, human checks, token limits, output validation, and scope limits keep autonomy from turning into expensive chaos. The more autonomy you give, the more these matter.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over to you: when you build an agent, which of these five takes the most work to get right?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How do you know if your AI app actually works?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You evaluate it. But most teams skip this step (or do it wrong) because “eval” feels vague. It’s not.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" plaintext;">Every good eval is a 3-step recipe.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Step 1: Pick a task. AI systems have different capabilities and dimensions to evaluate. For LLMs, it can be safety or math capability, in RAGs it can be grounding and retrieval, Pick one.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Step 2: Collect eval data. For every task, gather inputs paired with the right answer or expected behavior. A safety set pairs risky prompts with “refuse.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Step 3: Develop a grader. How do you decide if the output is good?</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Use code-based graders (if/else, unit tests) for things with a clear correct answer and patch passing unit-tests.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Use model-based graders (LLM-as-judge) for subjective tasks like safety.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Use human graders for edge cases and anything where nuance matters more than throughput.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Most production evals combine all three. Code-based for what’s cheap to check. Model-based for scale. Human-based for what matters most.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over to you: what’s the hardest thing about your 10 Career Traps (Thoughtful People Fall Into)

John Cutler

item.title: A Staff Engineer's Guide to Inventing Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Staff Engineer's Guide to Inventing Work

Sujith Jay Nair

“A big part of a staff engineer’s job in a platform team is to figure out what the team should build next - I like to call that “inventing work”. Thankfully, the signals that help us to invent work are already out there, and they arrive from four directions - from the systems, from the users, from your organization, and from the industry. What follows is a guide to reading each of them.”

#Strategy PlatformEngineering Staff+
item.description: A Staff Engineer's Guide to Inventing Work

item.title: How Do AI Coding Assistants Change The Shape Of Engineering Work Over Time?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Do AI Coding Assistants Change The Shape Of Engineering Work Over Time?

Lizzie Matusov

“Researchers at the University of Auckland surveyed professional software engineers who were very actively using using AI coding assistants during two time windows (October 2024 and April 2025). Each survey asked about time spent on six development tasks, perceived productivity, and the three DevEx dimensions, alongside open-ended questions about how the tools had changed their work.”

#Leadership AI DevEx
item.description: How Do AI Coding Assistants Change The Shape Of Engineering Work Over Time?

item.title: Hiring Breakpoints
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Hiring Breakpoints

“And there are a few important breakpoints to consider on the journey of growing your team. These might seem a bit obvious, but the important realization is that at these breakpoints hiring decisions are much more important, so if you keep them in mind as hard thresholds you’ll make better scaling decisions.”

#Management Scale Hiring

item.title: How We Made Claude 3x Faster In Two Weeks
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How We Made Claude 3x Faster In Two Weeks

“This August, we made the core user experience of Claude and the Claude desktop app about 3x faster in a two-week sprint. Users had been telling us it was slow, and they were right. We ran everything from a single Slack channel, with Claude in every thread.”

#AI CaseStudy Performance

item.title: Aho-Corasick
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Aho-Corasick

Colin James

“This post describes the construction of an Aho-Corasick automaton for the simultaneous matching of substrings within a sequence. I’m fond of this algorithm because it constructs an automaton from an existing tree data structure in a rather pleasant way.”

#DeepDive Algo
item.description: Aho-Corasick

0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>TTD (time to detect): one hour? </strong><span>The Firebase team never shared how long it took </strong><span>It took two hours and eleven minutes to roll out the fix, but due to caching (apps that had cached the incorrect server response served this cache for additional four hours, and so kept crashing for up to six hours.)</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Incident management basics</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Firebase team itself closed the outage with a short report effectively saying that there had been an outage, but they’d resolved it now, so thanks for your patience and have a nice day.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>This handling of a high-impact incident is absolutely </span><em>not</em><span> typical of Google, the company that coined the term ‘Site Reliability Engineer’ and wrote the SRE book.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>For one, Firebase never bothered updating its status page. </strong><span>Oddly enough, the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1543495f-25dd-4077-92bc-8e87776cc14b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">official Firebase status page</a><span> showed all systems green – despite the acknowledgement of the outage. Indeed, during it and afterward, they didn’t update the status page to indicate the lengthy outage:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Offer transparency on the stability of the service</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s worth asking: if an outage that takes down most (or all?) iOS apps using Firebase doesn’t warrant an update to the status page, then what does!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Will Google publish a postmortem for such a high-profile outage like this was? </strong><span>How did it happen, how did a backend change make it to production without basic validation and testing, and what’s changing so that  this category of bug doesn’t ship to production in the future?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We would know if the Firebase team published a postmortem, but it’s unlikely this will happen. </span><em>I asked Google if they plan to do so, but got no response after two days.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Given the customers of Firebase are all developers, it’s disappointing that Google seems unbothered about being transparent about how things went wrong and giving reassurance that they have learned from this outage in any way.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Either way, I hope Firebase audit their SDK to ensure that malformed backend data does not crash the SDK, and look through their release process so that backend changes are tested against the SDK, to avoid similar outages in the future.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: their outage because dev tools are not part of the DNA there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But with Firebase, I am surprised by this approach, indicating that it would be too much effort to give basic transparency to their customers (devs!) about why the platform stopped working for hours. Maybe Google is right and it doesn’t matter any more? Nothing will happen if they don’t update their status page during an incident, nor publish a postmortem afterward?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I’d like to think that standout incident management is where startups can do better than tech behemoths like Google and Meta, and build up the developer goodwill that Big Tech increasingly seems to not care about. As devs, we make decisions on which platforms we trust or not; platforms with no transparency or accountability after an outage feel less trustworthy to me than those that take this stuff more seriously.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">2. OpenAI’s platform play from AWS playbook?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>OpenAI hosted its annual DevDay this underline;">ChatGPT Code review</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8cad3ca0-1767-4691-815e-9beed650097d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Codex Security cloud</a><span>, and more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: href="https://substack.com/redirect/7cdb5e9f-8eda-4e8c-a3ba-2647bcbdb9e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: using ChatGPT credits. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/44b247b6-5d94-4830-a82f-cd29c6554106?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">X</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Here’s how OpenAI describes it:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“We’re making it easier to use your ChatGPT plan with other tools. Use your allowance across 16 partners including Cognition’s Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw, and Dactyl, and control how much each can use. Eligible OpenAI usage counts toward your plan limits. You can also sign in to a range of tools with your ChatGPT account to connect plugins faster and manage fewer passwords.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Until now, if you paid for ChatGPT or Codex – say, the $200/month plan – you have access to OpenAI’s models and Codex, and can also top up with credits to use more of OpenAI’s models. But going forward, you’ll be able to use “OpenAI credits” on AI products inside the likes of Notion, Vercel, OpenCode, and Amp.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Through a partnership with Baseten, OpenAI also allows the running of cheaper open models. </strong><span>Baseten is one of the leading inference providers, and OpenAI now natively integrates with it. A Baseten statement laid out what this means:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“OpenAI enterprise customers can now use existing OpenAI commitments for open models served by Baseten within Codex or via the Responses API. For enterprises, this means delivering even more intelligence per dollar through your existing OpenAI commitment.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>For now, there’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/364b76e8-f390-474c-b639-89a121835b03?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">an application process</a><span> for becoming a Baseten customer; afterward, you can use open models with zero data retention (ZDR.) Neat!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>OpenAI has made its own subscription a lot more valuable than those of other frontier labs. </strong><span>If you are a customer of Anthropic, you can only allocate spend towards Claude, and on Gemini it’s also only towards Gemini. But OpenAI lets you spend on open models and buy services from their partner network.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is a clever strategy; they no longer only compete on “who has the best (or cheapest) leading AI model?”, but also on how to spend AI budget efficiently. Clearly, OpenAI will be taking a  cut from spending going towards partners, and those partners will pay – at least initially! – because they’ll expect more business through it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong><span>OpenAI’s approach reminds me a bit of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a38eb5e1-30ac-4305-baf0-59b65d025628?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">AWS marketplace</a><span>: </span></strong><span>AWS also makes it very easy to purchase vendor solutions through its vetted </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a38eb5e1-30ac-4305-baf0-59b65d025628?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">marketplace</a><span>, and sends a single invoice. AWS also surely takes a cut from this: but it’s a winning setup for AWS customers who can integrate services easier with a click, for vendors who get more business, and AWS which provides a more feature-rich platform vs competitors, and generates revenue from taking a cut.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Maybe Anthropic will create its own “partner network”, or keep flying solo by ignoring the rest of the ecosystem. </strong><span>So far, it seems to be against  the idea of allowing Claude Code to integrate with other tools, or for a subsidized Claude subscription (on the $20 or $200 plans) to be used by any harness other than Claude Code. Anthropic also seems hesitant to adopt common standards across AI engineering; for example, it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c34d3fd-3d2e-48e5-b1da-cb6aec5eaff4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">took</a><span> 12 months longer than OpenCode, Codex, or Cursor, for Anthropic to add support for the AGENTS.md standard (!!). Until last month, Claude Code only supported the CLAUDE.md file, and it seems like it was Shopify CEO, Tobi Lutke’s, threat to dump Claude Code unless the harness did what every other harness already did, that forced Anthropic to reverse its position:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: Why CTOs and VPEs are quitting en masse: another take</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A CTO with 20+ years of experience and who reads Pragmatic Engineer, sent me some notes after reading the article ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12b84386-9875-440a-99c9-a6a30e81553f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Headed for the exit: the great engineering leader career break</a><span>.’ Asking not to be named, he set out what he sees as an important reason why so many senior engineering leaders are quitting their roles that was missing from the analysis:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“We have all learned how to build great things over time. Also how to find great people to work with. But we’ve also learned how hard it can be to build great things – and we’ve especially found out how hard it is to build great teams.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Fast forward to now. AI is changing how you build great things and how you construct great teams to build things. It’s happening fast. This is great!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>But this change makes builders want to </strong><em><strong>build</strong></em><strong>. </strong><span>We want to build again...so we can build more, and build faster with better tools, so we can increase the “talent density” of the team by doing more with fewer great people, and so on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s an amazing time to build things. And it’s only getting better. And people just want to be close to it. They want to build and see how far they can go with these new tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I have a bunch of friends in my social circle who are the “CTO drop outs” you speak of. </strong><span>More still who are moving from management to IC roles in large companies. And their stories are largely what I describe above. They simply see this as a truly exciting time to build.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the end, building is why they got into this field in the first place.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Basically, lots of CTOs or Head of Engineering folks are using AI to get back to the thing that made them get into computers in the first place. They’re “builders of things” at heart. To build bigger, more complex software, they learned how to build and lead teams; now with AI: what if you can build amazing things with a much smaller team? Lots of these folks would rather do this: start building themselves – then, later – with a much smaller, higher-leveraged team.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Thanks a lot to the CTO who reached out with this; do leave a comment if their experience resonates with you, on top of other </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12b84386-9875-440a-99c9-a6a30e81553f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reasons why folks are leaving</a><span>.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxODM2NzgzMSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTA4NzMzMTIsImV4cCI6MjEwNjQ0OTMxMiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.FU6cazAZdgmiy6r96ANi8mmsPj3u3ATil2TOZo9YJKM?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;">State is the information a system retains that affects its functionality in some way. For example, a website might keep track of users who have logged in. A document editor remembers the current text. A background worker logs which tasks it has completed and which ones are pending. A database stores the records written to it for as long as needed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Any useful software usually needs to manage state to carry out its intended functionality. The difficulty is keeping the state correct even as requests overlap, servers are added, machines fail, and software changes are deployed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Often, the common advice is to “make the application stateless”. But this advice needs explanation. It usually means making particular application servers easy to replace while putting their important state elsewhere. It doesn’t signify a complete absence of state. Understanding such a setup requires looking at why state exists, who owns it, and what happens when it becomes unavailable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we will look at why state is the hardest thing in software development and the multiple strategies that developers can use to manage He also worked on Gmail and distributed storage at Google.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this episode, Peter reflects on his journey from open source to Google to founding a database company, and we explore how to keep systems fast, reliable, and correct at scale, from Gmail’s early storage challenges to the tradeoffs in building distributed databases.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Peter tells us how AI has brought him back to writing code after his work shifted toward management, and why he believes AI can improve quality and multiply the impact of domain experts. We also consider the future of code review, and Peter has some advice about how to level up our engineering skills.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Peter</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/02342b0e-c289-4425-adab-b089e75207cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/0GzwuYGvKA4" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. Peter initially turned down Sergey Brin’s offer to join Google because of the commute. </strong><span>The very first version of the famous Google logo was made in GIMP, the free, open-source raster graphics and image editing software created by Peter and his college roommate Spencer Kimball.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: GIMP</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In 2001, Sergey reached out to Peter, invited him to an interview and then made an offer. But Peter said “no” because he lived in San Francisco and did not fancy the hour-long commute to Mountain View. Instead, he joined another startup, but that didn’t go anywhere. When Google reached out again, he took the chance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Peter almost did not ship GIMP after learning about an even more ambitious photo editor. </strong><span>Peter and Spencer worked hard on GIMP, but a few weeks before launching it, they saw an announcement about another program that promised to do everything GIMP did – and then some! Peter and Spencer felt discouraged but shipped anyway – and the rest is history. They never heard about the other ambitious project again. “There’s always going to be someone else working on your idea,” says Peter. “You can’t get dissuaded if they pre-announce it. To founders: assume that dozens of people have the same idea you have, but most won’t ship it! Know that it’s a competition; you’ve got to enjoy that aspect of it – don’t be afraid of it.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. B-trees were used in the first version of Gmail. </strong><span>Gmail launched on 1 April 2004, offering 1GB of email storage for free, an offer seen as so ridiculously generous at the time that most people assumed it was an April Fool’s joke! B-trees played a role in Gmail’s storage layer, thanks to storing email threads. Under the hood, each incoming message was matched to a thread using the search index. Threads and their unread counts were tracked by B-trees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>4. Colossus reduced Google’s file storage overhead by 33%, while increasing redundancy. </strong><span>Before Colossus, Google File System (GFS) stored three full copies of data. For Colossus, which became GFS’s successor, Peter and the team pioneered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eb16a47a-2e1e-417f-8baf-c6d832d739eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Reed–Solomon erasure coding</a><span> in a distributed file system. Data was stored twice, but redundancy increased!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>5. The fastest way to send a packet around the globe is through space!</strong><span> Peter keeps “speed of light numbers” in his head – similar to what turbopuffer founder Simon Eskildsen does with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cec4156a-a7a0-4aca-9569-393636a547ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">”napkin math” </a><span>calculations. For example, a network round trip within a zone went from milliseconds when Colossus was built to about 100 microseconds today (10x faster!). But sometimes the bottleneck is the speed of light, and as light speed is faster in a vacuum than anywhere else, that means the fastest global route is straight up to Starlink, across by laser, and then back down. Find out more in ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a7837eb1-5876-40cc-b4aa-e0d15267fd8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Delay is not an option: low latency routing in space</a><span>’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>6. Peter twice “beat” standard library data structures in performance terms.</strong><span> At Google, one of his colleagues noticed that std::map showed up in memory profiles. Peter looked closer and figured out that the std::map implementation is a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/72f16184-6992-49eb-b962-6d6f6ae0e2b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">red-black tree</a><span>, meaning every node has two pointers. Peter built a B-tree with nearly the same semantics which was both faster, due to spatial locality, and smaller because it used fewer pointers. They used this data structure inside Google. Peter also did something similar with Go’s map: it was performant, but he built a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdf73a48-de89-403a-aca3-ffee6b3b3748?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Swiss Table</a><span> implementation that was faster. That implementation later made it into the Go library, with the Go team helping to finish it!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>7. If you squint hard, everything in distributed databases and storage systems starts looking like a B-tree. </strong><span>These B-trees are a recurring theme in this podcast episode: the backend of Gmail, the std::map replacement, CockroachDB’s range index, etc. There’s even a paper on this phenomenon, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/456e5ca9-0184-4667-b223-c9b5089d4745?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Ubiquitous B-Tree</a><span>.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/98b771d1-5b13-42d3-bbb3-db5f4a5cd991?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Wikipedia</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>8.</strong><span> </span><strong>For consensus in a distributed database, at least three replicas are needed. </strong><span>With only one, recovery after it crashes isn’t possible. With primary and secondary replicas, neither one will know if the other received the last write following a crash. So, CockroachDB uses three replicas by default – and up to five for some system tables – and customers can add more, although this will result in higher latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>9. CockroachDB’s design was inspired by Google’s Colossus data storage system and Spanner. </strong><span>Colossus was append-only, meaning you could only add to files and not mutate them. Google’s distributed database, Spanner, was built on top of Colossus, and so Spanner’s design decisions came from Colossus’ append-only nature. But if you cannot update files and only append to them, it’s not possible to use B-trees as the database’s design structure since B-trees need the files to be updated. An ideal data structure for append-only filesystems is the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1ac17384-4095-49aa-b0dd-875150d33d3f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Log-structured merge tree</a><span> (LSM tree), where writes are appended to a log file for durability:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: RocksDB was the underlying storage engine that CockroachDB used in its early years. In 2019, Peter wrote and open sourced </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3f51ed9f-dd15-412f-a9c9-e26200a8c8a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Pebble</a><span>, which is now CockroachDB’s storage engine.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>10. Peter, the former C++ readability reviewer at Google, predicts we will stop reviewing code: </strong><span>At Google, every code change needs to be signed off for “readability” by a language readability reviewer, and Peter was a C++ readability reviewer for years. But these days, he’s reviewing less code and foresees this continuing. As he puts it: “What I’m finding is the agents are getting better; you’re having to give less and less scrutiny. I don’t know if it’s going to be this year or next, [but] we’re materially going to stop looking at the code in the same way we don’t look at assembly anymore.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>11. Non-engineers at Cockroach Labs built ~1,000 internal apps (!!) in a couple of months.</strong><span> Earlier this year, Cockroach Labs launched an internal platform for non-devs to build apps (think of it as an “internal Lovable”). Folks jumped at it; HR professionals built new tools they’d only dreamt of, while the CFO created the dashboards they’d always longed for, and many others too. Peter and the engineering team were surprised at this uptake, but it chimes with how OpenAI saw nearly all its non-engineers move almost their entire token spend from ChatGPT to Codex within just 4 months.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>12. Does “flow” still exist with AI? </strong><span>I asked Peter this, and he believes it does, but it’s different from the “coding flow” state: “It definitely feels a bit different. It’s maybe a bit less intense, but you’re managing more things cognitively. I’m thinking of ideas that normally would’ve taken me a week to experiment with. And I think of multiple of these experiments and then fire them off all simultaneously. [It feels as] if I was a college professor with a whole swarm of research assistants, and they’re all off doing things and it’s coming back </span><em>really</em><span> rapidly.”</span></p><h3 plaintext;">CodeAF is a new open-source software factory that sits on the Pareto frontier of cost, speed and quality. On DeepSWE it solved nearly 4× as many real GitHub issues as Claude Code on the same open model, and matched the official leaderboard result at half the cost.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It is built from the ground up for the next era of coding, where you stop chatting with agents and start directing them. This involves the use of tools. While MCP made it easier to expose these tools, there were a lot of other concerns that had to be handled in order to make it work at an enterprise level.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">DoorDash built a shared Agent Gateway to control how AI agents discover and use tools. plaintext;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why an AI Agent Needs Tools</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A language model can write a super-detailed explanation of how to investigate a software problem, but it doesn’t automatically have access to a company’s code repositories, incident reports, or production logs. We need to provide access to those systems through software. From the perspective of the model, these systems are like tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An AI agent is an application that uses a language model to decide which steps and tools to use while working on a particular task. A tool is a specific capability that the application makes available to the model. For example, searching documentation, reading a support ticket, and opening a pull request.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When the model selects a tool, the surrounding application uses the tool to execute the required operation and supplies the result back to the language model. The model can then use that result to decide what to do next. For example, an agent investigating a failed software build might retrieve the build logs, inspect relevant code, and use what it finds to explain the failure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some tools only read information. Others can also change something in a real system, such as updating a ticket or creating a pull request. This makes tool access a very important part of an agent’s design. It determines what the agent can learn and what it can eventually do with that learning. At DoorDash, these capabilities come from many places, including internal services, engineering systems, documentation platforms, and third-party software.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why MCP Is Not Enough</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Different systems or tools normally expose different interfaces. An API is a way for one program to request information or actions from another program. Without a shared approach, an AI agent application has to accommodate the particular interfaces of every tool it uses.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a common way to describe, discover, and invoke capabilities. An MCP server exposes tools, and an MCP client communicates with that server. The agent application uses an MCP client to access the tools.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/fc3e8921-93bb-439b-b9d9-156268d8bd0a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a8005ca4-2bb3-4c44-a0c8-8a90807d7cad_3836x2484.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":943,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":218918,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/217162538?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa8005ca4-2bb3-4c44-a0c8-8a90807d7cad_3836x2484.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is largely facilitated by two main operations:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The first is tools/list, which discovers the tools available from a server. The returned catalog gives the agent information about the available capabilities, including their names, descriptions, and expected inputs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The second is tools/call, which requests execution of a particular tool with the supplied inputs.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, a server might expose a tool for looking up an issue in the issue tracker. A discovery service tells the agent that this capability exists and how to request it. Invocation asks the server to perform a specific lookup.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Such a shared interface makes integration simple. However, DoorDash still had to decide which agents can use which tools, whose account an action should use, and how access should be monitored. A coding agent might need access to GitHub, Jira, code search, documentation, and systems that show production behavior. Each connection introduces decisions about permissions, credentials, available operations, and monitoring.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This makes the problem of tool access not just a matter of connection. Also, there are a bunch of company-specific rules that come into the picture here. MCP’s common interface doesn’t establish those company-specific rules. If every team implements these responsibilities independently, the same work gets repeated across many agents and servers. For example, one team might build an OAuth connection flow, another might develop its own secret handling, and another creates a different way to record tool usage. It becomes quite difficult to maintain consistent behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">DoorDash organizes this problem into three separate concerns:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Access: </strong><span>Deals with the identity and permissions behind a request. The platform needs to know who is calling, what that caller is allowed to do, and which credentials the downstream system requires. For example, an agent acting on behalf of an individual employee may need a different credential arrangement from an automated process running for an entire team.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Tool-surface Curation: </strong><span>This concern handles the capabilities presented to the agent. A downstream server might offer hundreds of tools, while a particular workflow only needs a small subset. DoorDash needed a way to select the relevant, approved tools instead of exposing the entire catalog.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Operations: </strong><span>This concerns what happens when these integrations run in production. Teams need to understand traffic, failures, response times, usage, and costs. They also need controls that prevent excessive requests from overwhelming downstream systems.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Agent Gateway brings all of these concerns and responsibilities into a shared platform. Let’s look at that in more detail.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Core Components of the Agent Gateway</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A gateway is a service through which requests pass before reaching their destination.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In DoorDash’s design, an agent sends its MCP requests to the Agent Gateway, which controls access and forwards approved requests to the appropriate downstream MCP server. Here, downstream simply means the system that receives a request after the gateway forwards it.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8cc9d012-ade5-4d5c-9c46-f12a2e21a5d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1b76d61c-a0fc-460b-ac04-f066d991e32d_4414x2890.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":953,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":533529,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/217162538?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1b76d61c-a0fc-460b-ac04-f066d991e32d_4414x2890.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="359.99313186813185" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7lqu!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1b76d61c-a0fc-460b-ac04-f066d991e32d_4414x2890.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are two core components involved here: a proxy and a registry.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The proxy handles requests as they arrive. It verifies the caller, checks permissions, applies rate limits, attaches the required credentials, and forwards the request. It also produces information used for monitoring and auditing. Since it handles the actual request traffic, it is considered part of the data plane.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The registry stores the information needed to govern the incoming traffic. This includes details about the registered agents and MCP servers, ownership details, connection settings, authentication modes, policies, discovered tool catalogs, and configurations that determine which tools are exposed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The registry is the source of truth for the control plane, which manages how the system should operate. The engineering teams use a management interface and API to configure the gateway, while the proxy applies the resulting configuration to requests.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This division between the two components separates the work of configuring access from the work of handling traffic. A tool owner can register a capability and attach policy through the control plane. The proxy then enforces that policy when the AI agents need to use the capability.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">DoorDash also separates internal workflows and external-facing use cases into different proxy planes. They share libraries and registry concepts. But they maintain separate trust boundaries. Think of it as a common governance approach without implying that every request passes through one physical proxy instance</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Verifying Who is Calling and What They Can Do</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Two closely related concepts play a key role in the Agent Gateway built by the DoorDash engineering team. These concepts are authentication and authorization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Authentication establishes the identity of the caller making the request. A request might come from a user, a software service, or an agent acting on behalf of a user. Authorization determines what that identified caller is allowed to do.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">These checks need more information than simply deciding whether someone can access an entire MCP server. A server may expose both harmless lookup operations and powerful administrative actions. The distinction between the two should be clear. For example, permission to search a repository should not automatically imply permission to use every operation the server provides.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">DoorDash’s agent gateway can evaluate permissions involving several pieces of context. It can consider the agent, the user, the requested tool, and the environment in which the request occurs. It can also distinguish access to read-only capabilities from access to capabilities that modify data. For example, a policy might allow an agent to read issue details on behalf of a user while preventing that agent from performing administrative operations. Another workflow might be allowed to run under a team identity, while a user-specific action requires the individual user’s authorization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The agent gateway carries the identity of the caller through the rest of the request process, including routing and recording usage. That makes it possible to attribute a downstream action to the context that caused it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Centralizing these decisions also gives DoorDash a shared place to change or revoke access if needed. Agent developers don’t have to encode security decisions in prompts. Also, each tool owner doesn’t have to rebuild the same gateway-level authorization logic.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Identifying the Caller is Different from Supplying Credentials</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Even after the agent gateway knows who is making a request and whether it is allowed, the downstream system may require its own credentials.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A credential is something used to establish identity or access, such as an API key or an access token. The identity used to enter DoorDash’s gateway and the credential required by a third-party service are separate parts of the request.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For instance, the gateway may recognize an employee through the internal identity system. However, a documentation provider may still require that employee’s authorization token before it allows access to their documents. There are four types of credential arrangements that are possible:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Internal Service Identity: </strong><span>This is an identity verified by the DoorDash infrastructure. It forwards verified caller context to internal services.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Gateway-held Token: </strong><span>This is a vendor or service token kept in gateway secret storage. It adds the token to the downstream request without giving it to the agent.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Per-user OAuth: </strong><span>This is for access that a particular user has granted to an external service. The gateway stores the grant securely, supplies the user’s token, and refreshes it when needed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Service Principal: </strong><span>This is a non-personal identity used by software or team automation. The gateway obtains or issues short-lived credentials through a gateway-managed team identity.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Credential injection means adding the appropriate credential to the outgoing request before forwarding it. The agent asks to use a tool. The gateway handles the credential needed to access the system behind that tool.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The design created by the DoorDash engineering team keeps raw downstream credentials, including vendor keys and OAuth refresh tokens, out of the agents. This gives the platform a central place to manage, rotate, audit, and revoke those credentials.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How a User Connects an Account During a Tool Call</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some tools need to act within a particular user’s account. For example, reading that user’s documents or updating a ticket as that user requires appropriate user authorization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">OAuth is a mechanism through which a user authorizes an application to access a service with specified permissions. The application receives tokens that it can use for the authorized access.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The access token is used when making requests. A refresh token, when issued, allows the application to obtain a replacement access token when the current one expires.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Before the agent gateway, the product teams within DoorDash tended to build their own connection flows and token storage. However, the gateway centralizes this work.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When a call needs authorization that is not yet available, the gateway starts the provider’s OAuth flow. After the user authorizes access, the gateway stores the resulting tokens in encrypted form and supplies the appropriate token on future calls.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For clients that support MCP elicitation, the gateway can ask the client to present a connection prompt while keeping the original tool request open. The user completes authorization in a browser. The gateway then obtains and stores the token, resumes the original request with that token, and returns the result from the tool.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" plaintext;">To clarify things here, elicitation is the protocol mechanism used to request the user interaction needed to continue the task. The user completes the provider’s authorization flow. However, the agent doesn’t receive the raw credential.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For clients without elicitation support, the gateway returns a structured response explaining that authorization is required, along with a connection URL. This gives the client a clear way to recover, even though it cannot use the same pause-and-resume interaction.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Agents Should See a Selected Tool Catalog</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Permissions determine which actions are allowed, but the tool surface shown to an agent also affects its behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Tool surface means the set of tools presented to an agent, including their names, descriptions, and organization. A server’s complete catalog may contain administrative functions, billing operations, destructive actions, and features unrelated to the agent’s task. Presenting all of those capabilities creates unnecessary choices. The model has more descriptions to interpret and more potentially similar tools to distinguish. The approach used by the DoorDash engineering team is to expose smaller, relevant catalogs that match the work being performed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are two mechanisms behind this: bundles and filters.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb238ce8-a148-4bd9-943d-fe10e5d663cd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction:
