to and changing with AI. We explore why Maggie starts projects with pens and notebooks, what distinguishes design engineers from other designers, and why understanding engineering constraints leads to better collaboration with engineers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also discuss how Maggie uses jigs to gain more control over AI agents, why human judgment and style still matter when models can generate designs, and how inconsistent AI capabilities can mislead us.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Maggie</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/403bcefe-b2f3-4218-b42b-952ddb4a4483?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/KZSzF0KEFRg" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Post-graduation, one potential career path led to a job inventing torture techniques for the US army. </span></strong><span>Maggie said ‘no thanks’ and resolved to work in tech instead. Maggie studied cultural anthropology and her background has helped her through her tech career to date. Software is built by people and relationships matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Maggie got a frontend engineering education from illustrating React tutorials. </span></strong><span>She spent four years as an illustrator at the developer education company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93fef6cf-936d-4262-8dc0-8ceb09e34aa5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Egghead</span></a><span>, rising to art director. To illustrate the lessons, it was necessary to understand what she was drawing: React components, useEffect, and JavaScript functions. </span><em><span>Note from Gergely: I followed Maggie’s work after her excellent illustrations work on Dan Abramov’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/347d69c9-94c3-4c6a-9390-75dabf33d4d0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Just JavaScript course</span></a><span>. Here’s an animated explainer by her for that course:</span></em></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="394" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8af1d675-3d71-4a19-8aae-b829cc5bef37?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1548e56b-dc1e-4c77-90b0-54c88ebd020e_394x270.jpeg","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":270,"width":394,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="394" height="270" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dn7v!,w_394,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1548e56b-dc1e-4c77-90b0-54c88ebd020e_394x270.jpeg" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Some folks believe the best UI interface already exists.</span></strong><span> In 2021, the AI startup where Maggie worked was trying to launch a new interface to speed up scientific research using LLMs – a year before ChatGPT was released. Months of intense work went into a “new UI for AI”, but it turned out that scientific researchers didn’t want innovations like infinite canvases with cards, composable Notion-like documents, and more. They wanted the same, simple tables they were deeply familiar and comfortable with! Maggie says the experience taught her that starting with a familiar primitive is sensible – even when innovating.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. The nomenclature matters! Also, problem solving is at the heart of design – just like in engineering.</span></strong><span> Maggie sees design and software engineering as related by being about problem solving. The difference lies in the materials. Coming up with the names and verbs to describe new things which will then be adopted and used by people can be hard work. Easy when building an online sneakers store, harder when building a new product for AWS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Notebooks are an important part of the designer’s toolkit. </span></strong><span>Maggie often starts her projects by sketching out ideas. She finds it faster to sketch out an idea by hand than to describe it to a tool like Claude Code. Plus, when you sketch out an idea physically, it will still be there in the notebook the next day. In contrast, if it gets put into a tool instead, it’s a lot harder to go back to it, dozens of prompts later!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Maggie regularly builds her personal Figma called “Jigs,” </span></strong><span>which is also the name of a woodworking device that helps with a specific job. She regularly asks a coding agent to build a prototype that has sliders and color pickers so she can tweak it in realtime, like having a personal Figma!</span></p><div Maggie has stopped looking at the code at work. </span></strong><span>When a PR is generated, she doesn’t look at the code, and this approach fits when building prototypes. Once she knows what to build, she composes a detailed spec, listing out how the agent will verify its work. Previously, she did keep an eye on the code, but that’s not needed with the new generation of models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Planning with AI agents breaks when there’s too much text. </span></strong><span>“I have this theory that planning is a really bad experience at the moment,” Maggie says. “An agent grills you with a set of choice A, B, or C questions a hundred times over. By question 20, you’re quite tired and your brain starts shutting down [because] you can’t make this many decisions in this short of time. Also, it told you A is recommended. Then you just start being like, ‘Yep, enter A, I agree with you.’”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. “Capability gaslighting” is when frontier models convince users they’re an expert but fail the same task the next day. </span></strong><span>Maggie coined the term “capability gaslighting” for how models impress users before failing badly soon afterward. Too often, we keep believing in models because we’re convinced they’re capable. The same is true for agents, so we should be vigilant when working with LLMs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. We need new types of artifacts for humans and agents to work better together, Maggie believes</span></strong><span>: “There’s this world that agents live in: there’s weights and models and skills and MCPs,” she says. “Then you have your human side: it is physicality and texture and light and materials and all these things agents don’t understand. Trying to find artifacts that allow us to meet in the middle and create stuff together is a really hard challenge because you’ve got two totally different types. I just find myself frustrated that agents cannot look over my shoulder, looking at my notebook and understanding what I’m drawing, and how they cannot help me move my ideas along.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. Engineers should try treating the AI agent as a patient tutor when learning about design: </span></strong><span>As engineers, we can ask AI agents to teach us about design: they’re good at explaining things like when to change up line height, what a good sidebar looks like, or how many characters to squeeze into a line, etc. In the past, acquiring product design skills was hard, but AI agents make it a bit easier</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>I hope you enjoyed this episode, and many thanks to Maggie for educating all of us engineers!</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe They can write code, summarize documents, and answer questions across many subjects. However, an application may still need something the model does not provide consistently. Its answers might omit important details, the way it classifies information might confuse similar categories, or its responses might ignore a particular expected writing style.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These things don’t mean that the model is not intelligent or doesn’t have knowledge. Often, it has the underlying capability but needs additional help applying it according to specific expectations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That is the purpose of customizing a model. One way is to follow clearer instructions and provide better information. But when those also leave gaps between the expectation and reality of the model, further training needs to be imparted. Techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA make that training more practical by reducing the resources needed to adapt an existing model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to look at the various strategies to customize and fine-tune a model.</span></p><div learning points in brief:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When instructions and information are not enough</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How fine-tuning changes a model</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LoRA: Learning a smaller set of changes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>QLoRA: Reducing the memory footprint of the model</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tuning the techniques into a training process</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>When Instructions and Information Are Not Enough</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The natural starting point in customizing a model is prompting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A prompt describes the task, identifies constraints, and specifies what a good answer should contain. For example, we can add examples of the type of answer we expect to give the model a clearer demonstration of the expected behavior. This approach is called few-shot prompting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This simple approach can be quite effective. The task of summarizing a document becomes more useful when it specifies which details matter and how the summary should be organized. Many applications need no customization beyond well-designed instructions and prompts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, instructions can’t provide information that is missing. If an answer depends on an internal document or a recently updated policy, the application must provide that material explicitly to the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the main technique for addressing this requirement. It finds relevant information in an external source and includes it in the model’s input. The model can then use that material when producing its answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prompting and RAG both work through the information supplied during a request. They can guide behavior in a big way, but they don’t ordinarily change the model’s learned parameters.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sometimes, recurring weaknesses remain. A model might still struggle with specialized document categories or keep producing summaries that highlight the wrong details. While adding more examples as part of every request may help, it also increases the amount of input the application must maintain and process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where fine-tuning offers a different option. In fine-tuning, we can train the model on many examples so that the desired behavior becomes more firmly learned as part of the model’s default behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is not an absolute division between behavior and knowledge. Fine-tuning can also teach facts. However, retrieval remains useful when information changes frequently, or answers must be traceable to an external source.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Fine-Tuning Changes an Existing Model</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you might be aware, a model’s behavior depends on billions of numerical values called parameters or weights. Many of these are weights that influence how information moves through the model’s calculations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During pretraining, these values are adjusted using large amounts of training data. A text-generating model learns to predict the next token, which is basically a piece of text such as a word, part of a word, or punctuation. This process helps develop broad language capabilities within the model. Models intended for conversation usually receive additional training to follow instructions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, fine-tuning continues from an existing model using a more focused dataset. Since fine-tuning builds on top of capabilities that are already present within the model, it reduces the amount of training required for specialization.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A common approach is supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In SFT, each training example contains an input and the response the model should produce. Examples might pair documents with approved summaries, messages with category labels, or programming requests with suitable code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During training, the model predicts the desired response tokens. The training process measures how well those predictions match the supplied targets. This measurement is called the loss. Backpropagation identifies how the trainable parameters influence that loss, and an optimizer adjusts them to improve the predictions going forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a model may initially answer a classification request with a long explanation. However, training examples that repeatedly pair such requests with short category labels encourage the model to aim for more direct responses. The same principle applies to the details provided in summaries or the conventions followed while generating code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Across many examples, these adjustments can increase the likelihood of desired behavior based on new inputs. Since the saved changes persist, future requests don’t need to include the entire training dataset in every input they provide.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Supervised fine-tuning does improve things, but it has limitations. Writing explicit examples for every possible scenario the model might encounter is impractical. This is where reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) provides further refinement. The process begins with the model generating multiple responses to various prompts. Human raters then rank these responses based on quality, helpfulness, and safety. These rankings train a separate reward model that learns to predict scores human raters would assign to any response.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed47f553-d9dc-4180-a663-38585cad1fcb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>SFT and RLHF describe how examples teach the model. On the other hand, LoRA and QLoRA describe how that training is carried out efficiently. The same instruction-response dataset can be used with these different approaches.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The more straightforward type of fine-tuning, known as full fine-tuning, allows every model parameter or weight to change. This provides flexibility, but is also quite expensive. Training must store the weights along with the information used to calculate and apply their updates. Also, intermediate results that were produced while processing examples must also be stored.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why a model that fits on a GPU for generating answers might require much more memory for full fine-tuning. Longer examples and larger groups of examples processed together only push the resource requirements higher.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, as we discussed, the model already has a pretty good grasp on the language aspects. Adapting it to a particular task may not require adjusting every parameter independently. This possibility leads to LoRA.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>LoRA: Learning a Smaller Set of Changes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA stands for Low-Rank Adaptation. It is a form of parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which means it reduces the number of parameters that training needs to update.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA keeps the original model weights frozen. They still perform their calculations, but training doesn’t modify them. Instead, small trainable components are attached to selected calculations inside the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These additions are called adapters. They learn adjustments that are combined with the original calculations. This way, the overall output generated by the model changes because the model now uses both its existing capabilities and the learned adjustments.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An adapter operates inside the model. It doesn’t wait for a completed answer and rewrite it afterward. Its adjustments influence the internal processing that eventually produces the answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These small components are implemented using two compact tables of numbers, called matrices:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The first creates a compact intermediate representation from the input for a calculation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The second turns that representation into an adjustment that can be added to the original result.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Training changes the values in these small tables.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The compact representation belongs only to the adapter. The original model still performs its full calculation, so the adapter doesn’t have to recreate all the capabilities the model already possesses. The reason this works is that changes often have shared patterns. If we want a model to write concise technical explanations, we don’t need it to relearn grammar, programming, and sentence construction. Much of that ability already exists within the original base model. Training simply needs to adjust how those abilities are applied.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The term “low rank” refers to representing such an adjustment through a limited set of coordinated patterns. These are learned numerical relationships, rather than explicit rules provided by a developer. Therefore, LoRA restricts how the model can change. This restriction saves resources, but it also creates a trade-off. A small adapter may be sufficient for one task and too limited for another.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A setting called rank controls the adapter’s capacity. Higher rank gives it more room to learn varied adjustments, while increasing its size and training overhead. Values such as 8, 16, 32, and 64 are possible starting points. But a higher rank is not automatically better.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the beginning of standard LoRA training, the adapters contribute no change. Therefore, the combined model starts with its original behavior. Their adjustments develop as training processes the new examples. LoRA can also target selected attention calculations, which help the model relate different parts of its input, as well as other transformations inside its layers. Targeting more locations provides additional opportunities to adapt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The savings are related to managing updates for a much smaller collection of parameters. The original model is still necessary and performs substantial computation. LoRA makes training more manageable without turning the underlying model into a tiny model.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>QLoRA: Reducing the Memory the Frozen Model Still Needs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA solves much of the expense of updating parameters, but the frozen base model still occupies memory. For a sufficiently large model, storing those weights can remain a major obstacle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>QLoRA, or quantized LoRA, addresses this by combining LoRA with quantization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Quantization stores numbers using fewer bits and a more limited set of possible values. It preserves an approximation of each original weight while discarding some numerical detail. This reduces storage, but it can also introduce errors into the model’s calculations. The overall model structure and parameter count remain the same. Each weight simply has a more compact representation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>QLoRA commonly stores the frozen base weights in 4-bit form. The adapters remain at higher precision, allowing training to make even finer adjustments to their values. Depending on the implementation, adapter parameters and calculations can use 16-bit or 32-bit formats.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6cedf28f-d911-4e9d-a77f-4bf1f3a22320?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We need to distinguish between storage and computation here. A weight can be stored compactly and reconstructed as a higher-precision value when needed for a calculation. This reconstruction creates an approximation, but doesn’t recover the complete detail discarded during quantization. QLoRA uses this approach to perform the base model’s calculations, combines their results with the adapter adjustments, and trains the adapters using the combined output. The original quantized weights remain frozen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Although training updates only the adapters, the original calculations still influence what those updates should be. Even if we freeze a part of the model, it is not removed from the learning process. Only the weights are not changed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the adapters learn alongside the quantized model, they adapt to that actual combination. They can help recover task performance affected by compression, although they cannot be assumed to correct every quantization error.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For a fixed memory budget, this can make it possible to customize a larger model than ordinary LoRA would allow. The original QLoRA work has shown great savings, but the practical requirement still depends on the model, length, batch size, and training implementation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Compressed weights are only part of training memory. The system still needs adapters, their update information, intermediate results, and working space. Lower memory use also does not guarantee proportionally faster training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA and QLoRA are therefore closely related. LoRA reduces how much must be trained, while QLoRA also reduces the space occupied by the frozen base model.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Turning the Techniques Into a Training Process</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first decision is to choose a suitable starting model. The model should already perform reasonably well in the required language and task. This is because a model that struggles with basic instructions or lacks the necessary capabilities will not do wonders even after customization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before training, we need to establish a baseline using a carefully developed prompt. This provides a clear picture of the remaining problems and a reference for measuring improvement.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Next, we need to prepare examples that demonstrate the desired behavior. For extraction, include messages with different wording, missing information, and details. For summarization, provide varied documents and consistent examples of how it should be structured.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Correctness is important here because training rewards agreement with the supplied answers. If similar inputs receive contradictory labels, the model can receive conflicting guidance. If approved summaries contain unsupported claims, those claims also become part of the behavior being taught.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Next, we need to prepare separate training, validation, and test sets:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training examples cause parameter updates.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Validation examples help compare settings and choose a saved version of the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Test examples provide a final assessment after those decisions.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Duplicate or closely related examples should not leak across these groups.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The training configuration then controls capacity, update size, and resource use. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Rank and adapter placement determine how much adjustment LoRA can learn. This learning rate controls the size of training updates. Excessively large updates can destabilize learning, while very small ones can produce little progress.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Batch size describes how many examples are processed together. Larger batches generally require more memory. Gradient accumulation allows several smaller batches to contribute to an update. This helps a lot when memory is limited.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Another memory-saving option is gradient checkpointing. It keeps fewer intermediate calculation results and recreates some of them when needed. This trades additional computation for lower memory use and can complement LoRA or QLoRA.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Training duration is measured in epochs, where one epoch means one pass through the training dataset. One to three epochs can be an initial experiment, but repeated exposure isn’t always better. Training longer can make the model overly dependent on the examples it has already seen. This problem is called overfitting. A warning sign for this is when performance on training examples improves alongside worsening performance on validation examples. The useful checkpoint may come before the final training step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The evaluation process should measure the actual task. For example, classification needs correct labels, extraction needs correct values, and summarization needs faithful coverage of important details. Well-formed output alone doesn’t establish correctness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, we need to check the capabilities the application still depends on. An adapter can improve one behavior while weakening another, even though the original weights remain frozen. The combined model’s behavior has changed, so it must be evaluated as a whole.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Using the Specialization in an Application</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA training produces adapter weights that can be saved separately from the base model. These files are generally much smaller than a complete model, but they require the compatible base checkpoint to function.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Keeping adapters separate makes it easier to manage different specializations. Where the serving software supports it, the same base model can be used with different adapters for different tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another option is to merge the adapter’s learned adjustments into the base weights. This produces a standalone customized model and removes the need for separate adapter calculations. The resulting file contains the full model, so it loses the storage advantage of an adapter-only file.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Merging and quantization support depend on the implementation. We need to evaluate the exact version that will be deployed, since changing its numerical representation can affect results.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application can still use prompts to specify the current task, RAG to supply relevant information, and validation code to check outputs. Fine-tuning improves learned behavior while these other features continue handling their own responsibilities as before.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Fine-tuning is useful when a model has broad capabilities but needs more reliable specialization. It learns from demonstrations and reflects recurring response patterns more firmly in the model’s behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA makes this less expensive by learning compact adjustments while preserving the original weights. QLoRA reduces the memory requirement further by storing those frozen weights at lower precision.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Neither technique replaces good examples or careful evaluation. The goal is a measurable improvement on new inputs, at a cost the application can support. A clear task, a suitable starting model, and representative training data matter as much as the choice of training method.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: href="https://substack.com/redirect/38ce79e0-285d-4fa1-baf7-576ca504ca96?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: This is an evening with OpenAI, Linear and DoorDash and myself, organized by Sentry. We get into what AI-augmented automations they’re running in prod, and how it’s going, in an off-the record and raw conversation. Seats are limited, but as a paid subscriber, I’m aiming to prioritize your RSVP: please you use the code TODO</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI is changing how us software engineers build software, and developers’ tool preferences are rapidly evolving with it – like how AI coding harnesses have gotten very popular. Likewise, future versions of the world’s leading operating systems look certain to feature more support for agentic tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To find out how things are changing, we talked with the folks at tech giant Microsoft who shared in detail their plan for Windows, and how AI will play a part. It comes after the company’s previous AI efforts led to it being dubbed “Microslop” by some users online.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Windows team’s vision is opinionated and includes building new agentic primitives, alongside reversing some decisions that have annoyed engineers. Microsoft wants developers who have shunned the system to return. The big question is: will it succeed?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For more, check out a previous article on how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa762701-df41-4c7f-bb51-025eae16539a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the leading Linux distribution, Ubuntu, is changing, thanks to AI</span></a><span>, with a focus on hardware support for GPUs, NPUs and DPUs, a bet on local-first LLMs, and a focus on AI developer tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How many devs use Windows anyway? </span></strong><span>It’s hard to get exact numbers, but macOS appears far more popular at startups than Windows, while Linux may also be on track to overtake Microsoft’s OS in developer popularity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent identity & discovery.</span></strong><span> Windows ships with native support for agent identification, plus a centralized registry of locally available MCP servers to be included with the OS.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Isolate agentic tools.</span></strong><span> Microsoft is building an OS-agnostic isolation mechanism that should make it easy for developers to build agents that run tools safely.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Running models locally</span></strong><span>: Windows is betting big on local models. WindowsML is a new hardware abstraction layer for building and running local AI models across GPU, NPU, and CPU. The OS aims to ship Small Language Models (SLMs) without requiring an NPU in the future. We’ve also seen an impressive demo of a local model running on a Surface laptop using NVIDIA chips.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building agents on Windows:</span></strong><span> one goal of the OS is to allow building of agents with opinionated frameworks and libraries that devs can just assume are available.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More dev-friendly</span></strong><span>: Windows was plagued by questionable product decisions that resulted in a cluttered Start menu and search, to the chagrin of many developers who lost interest in the OS. Microsoft wants them back and is addressing criticisms – </span><em><span>finally!</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Linux on Windows (WSL): </span></strong><span>Windows ships with an embedded Linux called Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). It’s proving quite popular with devs. Windows embracing Linux might just be the strategy to get devs to switch from both native Linux and macOS, as counter-intuitive as this strategy sounds.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows & hardware:</span></strong><span> since its early days, Windows has gone out of its way to support a wide variety of hardware. The OS was x86-based from the beginning, but Windows on ARM is starting to finally look like a good alternative. A look into why ARM support took so long, and the upcoming NVIDIA collaboration.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve talked with people on the Windows team to learn about the thinking behind Microsoft’s strategy for the operating system: Pavan Davuluri (EVP, Windows and Devices), Scott Hanselman (VP, Member of Technical Staff, Microsoft CoreAI and GitHub), and Logan Iyer, (CVP, Windows Platform and Developer). </span><em><span>Many thanks for your time!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: Agent identity & discovery</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the operating system level, agents increasingly look like regular users. Their sessions can last hours, use multiple programs, and use OS resources like the UI and clipboard. Windows allows developers to build agentic programs that are distinguishable from users.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Agent identification</span></strong><span> is enabled through </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dcca0083-34f5-46d6-82e9-2815fd9b1f8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Entra ID</span></a><span>, Microsoft’s tool for centralized identity management in Windows. When an agent has a local identity, it acts as if it is another user on the system as visible in the Task Manager. Below, tasks are grouped by user, and there are two users in the task manager: kirupach (a human) and V9-G4 (an agent). All observability of human users is now available for agent users as well.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure underline;"><span>ODR</span></a><span>) is the centralized place where agents register and discover available MCP tools. ODR manages and runs MCP servers locally, and also comes with connectors for core operating system components like the File Explorer or System Settings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say you want to build a specialized Photo Organizer Agent; the organizer agent organizes photos in the user’s Photos folders by theme and starts by running an image classifier to understand photos’ themes, then puts them in the relevant folder, such as ‘</span><em><span>parties</span></em><span>’, ‘</span><em><span>outdoors</span></em><span>’, ‘</span><em><span>baby photos</span></em><span>’, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As such, the Photo Organizer Agent needs the ability to read and change the user’s local files, which starts with Windows ODR finding an MCP connector for the file access capability. After discovering File Explorer, the agent uses File Explorer MCP to access and modify files in the user’s Photo directory.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: This is a useful choke point because it enables Windows to detect potentially dangerous behavior. However, this proxying behaviour is as yet unconfirmed by Microsoft, so it remains to be seen how they use it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>3. Isolate agentic tools</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tools are external programs that an agent uses to perform actions on the operating system, such as native OS tools, third-party app calls, or even programs written by an agent. Granting agents rights to execute tools potentially means code execution, so it’s essential the agent tools run in isolation to ensure the user’s files and session aren’t reachable by agentic tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft Execution Containers</span></strong><span> (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aef28adb-0819-406e-9e24-0aec5ff80526?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>MXC</span></a><span>) is a new, in-development agent containment technology by Windows. Developers can use MXC to spawn agentic tools in isolated environments called sandboxes, and agent access within the sandbox environment is configured through MXC </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/02a904fa-9ced-4046-a278-14d9b478a820?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>containment policies</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Containment policies are JSON-based config files that describe network, filesystem, UI, and execution restrictions. The image below illustrates how MXC works:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 different containment tech & OSes</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say you’re building an agentic application like OpenClaw. This application will necessarily have to use tools to do its job and can use file operations, web operations, shell commands, and more. These are potentially dangerous operations, as OpenClaw executes them through MXC’s spawnSandboxFromConfig() method, which spawns a new contained process in which said tools can run safely. The process containment technology used depends on the containment policy config. MXC doesn’t do the containment itself and uses multiple existing containment technologies for that; for example, on a Mac, it would use </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f8888044-39f9-4d8e-b3a6-00624c94b39b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>seatbelt</span></a><span>, a process containment layer built into the Mac OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Speed versus safety tradeoff: </span></strong><span>some containment mechanisms are faster to start and cheaper to run than others. For example, starting a new process is faster than starting a new Windows session or a new virtual machine. At the same time, running a new process in the existing user’s Windows session potentially exposes the user’s filesystem to the new process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MXC allows developers to adapt the containment level to the sensitivity of the operation being run. Multiple containment levels are available in Windows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Process containment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Session containment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running WSL containers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lightweight Hyper-V containers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Full virtual machines</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Choosing the right level of containment is a trade-off between the blast radius and speed of execution. border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The policy object specifies how the containerized workload should be constrained. It specifies network, UI, filesystem restrictions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The createConfigFromPolicy step configures the whole container. It takes the containment policy object, the chosen isolation level (“process”), and names the container.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The app then manipulates what gets executed in the “WHAT RUNS” step</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Finally, spawnSandboxFromConfig() runs the container and processes its output.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenClaw for Windows ships as a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b922c8d3-d229-48e5-a0f5-e2d24e0aab68?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>native app</span></a><span> and is one of the first agents to adopt MXC for isolation. Configuring the MXC containment in OpenClaw for Windows is packed as a standard windows settings screen.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: chores, and how MXC provides finegrained control over agent isolation. MXC is under development, but already runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Developers therefore get a unified way of containing external tools across operating systems.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Running models locally</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e132cbc6-d8f0-41e5-b847-5a7712c250f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Windows ML</span></a></strong><span> is a hardware-agnostic layer for running AI models locally on Windows. Its goal is to do for AI what DirectX did for computer graphics: abstract away hardware complexity, regardless of the underlying model’s architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows ML is Microsoft’s second attempt at building a hardware-agnostic layer for running ML models. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f6c2145-b586-4925-8bed-f94132c565b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>DirectML</span></a><span>, the first attempt, is a library for running machine learning tasks on GPUs built on top of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a22ab27-4ff2-4a8f-b3b8-b11afb09ada1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>DirectX 12</span></a><span>, Microsoft’s graphics library used for running games on Windows, released in 2019.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, an obvious question is how is Windows ML different? They say that Windows ML offers two improvements over DirectML:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>#1: Higher level abstraction & better hardware coverage</span></strong><span>. DirectML is a low-level library where developers have to manually build the inference pipelines from simple mathematical operations, worry about memory layout, etc. Being based on DirectX, DirectML only worked with GPUs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, Windows ML is based on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c653bbd-199d-4690-8d4a-47440d36afb5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Open Neural Network Exchange format</span></a><span> (ONNX), an open format for representing and running neural networks. Neural networks built with all popular machine learning frameworks can be converted into the ONNX format called ONNX graph and run on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eabf5226-275d-45c9-900f-59fc4261fedf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>ONNX runtime</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>ONNX runtime is an open source, cross-platform system for training and running neural nets defined in the ONNX format. Windows ML provides developers a framework that runs on a broader range of silicon, including GPUs, NPUs, and CPUs from all major vendors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>#2: No driver-update bottleneck:</span></strong><span> Windows ML wraps the ONNX runtime and abstracts away the hardware-specific runtime optimizations by providing hardware-agnostic APIs. Each hardware vendor implements this API for its own hardware through the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9e899d05-155d-49f7-9979-7b998c18acc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Execution providers</span></a><span> (EPs) concept. With DirectML, new runtime optimizations had to be done via driver updates which took six months to get meaningful adoption.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows ML loads EPs when they are needed, depending on the user’s hardware. For example, if a user has an NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPU, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7a375fca-fa6f-4dc1-8224-54fe25446e08?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the NVIDIA Tensor RTX execution provider</span></a><span> is downloaded and used to maximize GPU performance. Hardware vendors build and submit PEs to Microsoft for certification and testing before they can be used with Windows ML. Most execution providers </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dfcb20c7-ce5f-4ac0-a8bf-a74a8a55026f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>available today</span></a><span> are also available on GitHub.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: underline;"><span>Small language models</span></a></strong><span> (SLMs) are embedded within the operating system. Without them, developers would have to ship models with their apps, or call cloud-based models. On top of incurring app running costs, it can also add lag to the app, whereas with embedded models developers can assume the models are already there, and use them as any other local library. </span><br><br><span>For example, </span></span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b40816a9-cb00-495b-b43e-37c33f166dfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the Aion-1.0-Instruct model</span></a><span> is built into Edge, Microsoft’s web browser. Accessed through the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6f3314d3-8b53-4b74-ad0e-cb983d8c4c28?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Prompt API</span></a><span>, Aion model allows developers to build apps like sentiment analysis with a few lines of code. underline;"><span>Source</span></a><span>)</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even a simple web application can now have LLM-powered features like sentiment analysis without having to continuously pay for tokens. The demo is JavaScript-only, but versions for native apps and other languages are also expected to be available when it’s released.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teams being able to run their own models is becoming increasingly important, especially in the corporate sector, driven by escalating costs, mode availability questions such </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/443fde75-4527-46f5-935f-839f54a8c3be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as those recently raised with Fable</span></a><span>, and compliance issues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Running models locally also unlocks a hybrid approach, which is well aligned with a trend among tech companies we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/362cd763-34b9-488c-a6ee-4dca0b487c44?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>recently covered</span></a><span>, where tech companies have successfully shifted their LLM workloads to cheaper models for simpler requests, and only use frontier models for advanced reasoning. By running models locally, some agentic jobs could be executed with local LLMs, and more complex jobs delegated to a cloud-hosted frontier model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Running local models on a next-gen Surface laptop with NVIDIA GPUs is impressive. </span></strong><span>At Microsoft, Scott Hanselman showed us a pre-release Surface laptop with NVIDIA GPUs running Qwen as a local model, hooked up to GitHub Copilot. This local model churned out tokens at a rate of ~40 tokens per second! Once such laptops become widely available, coding-related use cases could become a lot more viable, running locally.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>5. Building agents on Windows</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Besides Windows being agent-friendly, Microsoft is also investing in the agent building toolchain to simplify agentic app development by providing a rich agent building framework.</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f45d3b79-6ca8-4a5e-9afd-28256feca533?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft Agent Framework</span></a></strong><span> (MAF) is a C#, Python, and Go library designed to make it easy to build agents on Windows. More than just a wrapper around LLM APIs, the framework supports agentic primitives like tools, multi-turn conversations, persisted memory, and even a workflow engine. It’s the main option for .NET developers and integrates well with agentic primitives in Windows mentioned earlier. The following snippet illustrates how easy it is to use MAF primitives:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure
