functions that your agent can then use as tools, which is explicitly mandated via instructions passed in the system prompt. You don’t have to stitch together old message exchanges to keep the agent’s context up to date; the built-in session capability handles it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MAF natively supports all the above-mentioned agentic primitives that the OS ships with. Developers can use it to build native agentic apps for Windows which in turn comes with useful agentic primitives built into the OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows being an opinionated runtime environment for agents has a few advantages for developers who build agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Simpler to build Windows-native agents.</span></strong><span> Developers can assume certain agentic capabilities in the OS. For example, local MCP capabilities can be discovered and registered via ODR, and there’s a simple way to contain tool execution.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Support to run local LLM models.</span></strong><span> Windows ML will make it easy for developers to include custom local AI models within their apps. Previously, developers had to consider hardware variants and bundle different SDKs with their app. Windows ML should abstract all of that away.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Company-level agent administration.</span></strong><span> Larger companies can have control over agents in their enterprise. Whitelists dictate which agents can run, limit what access they have, and have observability of agents in the network.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>6. More dev-friendly</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As alluded to by the existence of terms like ‘Microslop’, Windows isn’t such a popular operating system among software developers these days. This is a change from when the OS couldn’t be avoided during its </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62fd7e3d-9fe9-43e8-886f-28b2d68320d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>XP</span></a><span> era, when Windows enjoyed a 90+% market share. But that changed as apps transitioned to web and mobile, driven by two forces:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Switching operating systems easier than ever</span></strong><span>. Most modern apps are web based and run on any OS. Before, when considering a switch to a new OS, you had to check if your favorite desktop apps worked. This is no longer an issue as modern desktop apps are on the web, or use cross-platform frameworks like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe742241-c5f2-41cf-a6d8-322bb71f128f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Electron</span></a><span>.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows got less developer-friendly. </span></strong><span>Windows became less configurable over time, with stricter requirements on what users could do – exactly the things developers dislike. Also, command line support lagged behind Unix-based operating systems, and Microsoft kept ignoring developers’ configurability complaints.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, developers were frustrated with Windows as they felt it wasn’t prioritizing their use cases. For example, OS configurability, flexibility, and system details that developers value were largely ignored:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Mandatory Microsoft accounts: </span></strong><span>these became compulsory with Windows 11. Windows is the only OS to mandate a vendor-specific account to use an OS. With macOS, an Apple account is only needed to use Apple services; the OS can be used without one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Clutter and ads: </span></strong><span>The start menu and Windows search grew cluttered with irrelevant content like app suggestions, web search results, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7edbd9a2-9cd5-4e6f-93b4-a8a7131aa312?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>even ads</span></a><span>, with no way to change things.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of customization:</span></strong><span> With Windows 11, customization of the taskbar’s size, position, auto-hide, and similar tweaks, were no longer possible</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since then, the Windows team seems to have gotten the memo that devs dislike all the above changes, and Windows chief Pavan Davuluri </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4862ca6c-3638-40f0-b15f-375f271ac06d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>committed</span></a><span> to making Windows better for developers. Now, there’s now less clutter in the start and search menus, and Windows simplified its most used menus. Non-critical features are now optional:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start menu size can be changed and no longer has to occupy the whole screen, which is critical on smaller laptops.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Various tips and app recommendations can now be removed from the Start menu</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Here’s an example of how broken Windows Search was, until recently. </span></strong><span>Below, a user searches for a text file (“New Text Document”) that contains the word “motorola”. Before, on the left-hand side, Windows Search returned too many irrelevant web results and suggestions. But after a recent change, it now returns only the relevant document.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure fire-and-forget operation. The script will make the necessary changes to the OS and even handle multiple reboots for settings that need it. The overall operation can last an hour or more, but the whole process is hands-off for the user.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft Account still required:</span></strong><span> Frustratingly for some users, a fresh Windows installation </span><em><span>still</span></em><span> requires a Microsoft account. While </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e10dcf87-19ea-45e1-9004-16f96c826e25?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>multiple</span></a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/de06a652-9755-4b2a-9b6f-a0ad31b4f499?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>bypasses</span></a><span> exist, we fail to see how such a strict requirement can make Windows attractive to devs when no other OS mandates a vendor-specific account just to install it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Being forced to log into an account like this is annoying, but the privacy controversy over the ‘Recall’ feature dealt a major blow to Microsoft’s already-damaged reputation with devs: </span></strong><span>In May 2024, Microsoft </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45207783-e6b0-4436-b299-ed3baf882f54?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> Recall, a Windows feature that allows users to search their previous activity. Recall took screenshots of the desktop every few seconds, indexed them, and made them searchable. It was marketed as a photographic memory for a computer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There were two major problems with this:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No ability to turn it off:</span></strong><span> Microsoft </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22b8e125-6f4f-4d60-8fd1-e5b96e1685a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wanted</span></a><span> to make the feature non-removable, using resources on all machines, whether or not a dev wanted to use the privacy-invading feature.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Comical security approach</span></strong><span>: Recall shipped with a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c480b6f-56f7-420c-b561-f58b47451d18?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>serious security flaw</span></a><span>. Screenshots did not remove sensitive information like banking data or other personal data, and all the information was kept in a local SQLite database in plaintext! That meant any local app or rogue user could read the data without the user’s consent or knowledge.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s unclear why Microsoft thought it would be acceptable to ship a poorly implemented, privacy-invading feature without an opt out. Microsoft later </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ac93ff8c-7c10-46c9-b898-5ab036f4a8e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>cancelled</span></a><span> the June 2024 general launch of Recall, and the final version was released to the public in April 2025, as an opt-in, non-mandatory, feature. But much damage was already done. Why would devs trust an OS vendor that shipped core OS features so carelessly, and only changed course after large – and predictable! – public uproar?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>7. Linux on Windows (WSL)</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Historically, developer tools were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5d7f975b-df1e-4947-ad42-cb83740efac7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft’s strong suit</span></a><span>; after all, its very first product was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ac896b4-08c2-400f-807a-423bf9465567?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>BASIC interpreter</span></a><span>. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Visual Studio was the gold-standard IDE for building desktop applications: fast and snappy at a time when competing IDEs like Eclipse or NetBeans were painfully slow. Until around 2010, the Visual Studio debugger was the industry standard for debugging tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Microsoft’s development tools became less popular as the tech industry focus moved from desktop apps to web apps, and later to mobile apps. The issue was that Microsoft’s tools were Windows-only, while web and mobile apps were built using open source technologies. So, developers increasingly chose Mac or Linux. In response, Microsoft is making Windows more Unix friendly to try and win developers back.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) has addressed the issue by shipping Windows with an embedded Linux since 2016. With WSL, Linux is accessible in Windows by typing wsl in the command prompt. Previously, running Windows and Linux on the same machine required </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a064d46-018d-4bfc-bb73-95df2bc5a334?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>dual-booting</span></a><span>, and during that process the user had to pick which operating system to use. Switching back to the other OS required a reboot, and sharing data between the two operating systems was cumbersome. Linux could read or write Windows disks, but not vice versa.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>WSL doesn’t just run Linux inside Windows. It has also allowed running native Windows apps from WSL for a few years now. For example, let’s say you have the following a web server access log file:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>WSL is proving popular with developers.</span></strong><span> Scott Hanselman told us:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Linux on Desktop is already happening, it’s just running inside Windows.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jon Seager, VP Engineering at Canonical working on Ubuntu </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/de2c4526-d7e3-4ff0-9132-55e30e5f75b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>told us a similar story in April</span></a><span>, of Ubuntu adoption through WSL growing significantly faster than general Ubuntu desktop adoption, and how it expects more Windows-based machines to run Ubuntu than “native” machines running the Linux distribution!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are a few reasons why WSL became popular with devs:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use the same stack that production runs on. </span></strong><span>Most servers run on Linux. Building software for Linux on Windows without WSL is possible, but in most cases it adds a layer of unneeded complexity. Developers want to build in an environment that resembles production as much as possible, and WSL makes this possible.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Work on a gaming PC: </span></strong><span>many devs still have Windows boxes, but they just don’t use them for work. Instead, they’re for gaming because Windows has a big videogame library. WSL allows them to use the Windows box the same way they would use their work computer. Since the gaming PCs often have good GPUs, they can be used as CUDA dev boxes through WSL. Building with CUDA is possible without WSL, but the production environment is Linux.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Developing for Linux services</span></strong><span>: as one example, building Kubernetes applications on Windows previously meant running virtual machines inside Windows. VMs are slow and take up more memory than running the service in the OS itself. With WSL, Kubernetes can run on Windows without this VM overhead.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft’s goal is to make Windows a place where getting developer tasks done is easy. A task can require a Linux or a Windows tool, or a combination of both, but it should still be easy. As further evidence that Microsoft is committed to this, Windows recently added a native </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/99396ea1-a421-43d5-89a2-11d40a7157a2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>coreutils implementation</span></a><span>. With this, it’s possible to run standard UNIX utilities like cat, head, tail, sort, and uniq inside of a Windows terminal, even without WSL.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Containers are another Unix primitive coming to Windows.</span></strong><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/90762aab-5009-4eeb-8a2c-4dfe887e5f30?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Containerized apps</span></a><span> have been an industry standard for building and shipping software since the late 2010s, and the launch of Docker. Windows has supported Docker Desktop through WSL since ~2019. But the recently announced </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/416b6705-e9b1-4ea5-807d-9d970f6c6e0a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>WSL Container</span></a><span> takes Docker support in Windows further:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It provides a Windows native drop-in replacement for the docker CLI</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It comes with an API that Windows apps can use to manipulate containers directly from the application code</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The common theme of these launches is that Microsoft is trying to make Windows interesting to developers once more by supporting both Unix and native Windows-style development. Making standard Unix tools available certainly is a big step forward. However, it’s still necessary to address other accumulated grievances which devs have.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>8. Windows & Hardware</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From the 1990s, Windows had a symbiotic relationship with Intel called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2453132e-208a-40ce-b411-673847793dcc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Wintel</span></a><span>, which was an interplay of:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>New CPUs enabling newer versions of Windows: most famously 386 CPUs enabling Windows 3.0</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Windows requirements driving hardware consolidation. Most notable examples included </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62821160-92f8-42cd-8ad2-64f75cffd3c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>PnP</span></a><span> for automated hardware installation with Windows 95, UEFI Secure boot with Windows 8, TPM 2.0 security standard with Windows 11</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It wasn’t always an easy relationship. For example, when CPUs became 64bit, Intel built a new architecture with its Itanium CPUs, and AMD chose a backward-compatible x64 architecture. Windows ran without changes on AMD’s design and Itanium required all software to be rebuilt for it. Windows adoption helped AMD’s approach to win out, and Intel discontinued the Itanium line in 2021.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Windows-on-ARM saga</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>ARM processors are more energy efficient than x86 CPUs, while ARM based laptops have longer battery life, and are quiet since they do not need fans for cooling. Windows has been tied to x86 CPUs since the 1990s, so running the OS on ARM is challenging as supporting ARM processors requires more than just recompiling the OS from source code. It also requires changing the kernel architecture to run efficiently on them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Needing so many changes is why it took multiple attempts and more than a decade to get Windows to run well on ARM with good app availability. Here’s an overview of the Windows-on-ARM story:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows RT (~2012)</span></strong><span>: a tablet-focused fork of Windows never meant to fully replace it on laptops. There was no way to run standard Windows apps on Windows RT, so the platform didn’t get traction and was later abandoned.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows 10 on ARM (~2017)</span></strong><span>: Microsoft went for full x86 compatibility through a realtime translation engine. The translation performance was poor and excessively drained batteries when running x86 apps, and couldn’t execute x64 apps at all. The industry largely abandoned 32-bit software, so popular apps like Adobe Photoshop and web browsers like Chrome couldn’t even run on this OS. This approach was abandoned for Windows 11.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows 11 on ARM (~2024):</span></strong><span> a new emulation engine called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/16faa744-1b44-4b5d-901c-7f61f33e4938?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Prism</span></a><span> improved the emulation performance and finally supported 64 bit applications. This makes apps running in emulated mode more responsive, making the ARM transition possible.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Interestingly, Linux has similar ARM adoption problems, despite the fact that most of its software is already open source. While open source apps are available for ARM64 Linux, the main problems are with proprietary, closed-source apps. For example, Chrome became available for ARM on Linux in early August 2026.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of the problem with the Windows-10-on-ARM attempt was that the chips these machines were running were in essence mobile phone CPUs; underpowered and unsuited for the heavy workloads expected of a Windows workstation. With Windows 11, Microsoft partnered with Qualcomm and later, NVIDIA, to design stronger chips, which are natively equipped with NPUs and are part of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c7af742-8cd5-48cb-9d16-9f8ae371cb1c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Copilot+ PC specification</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Copilot+ PC specification was introduced in 2024, with the goal to define the baseline for what a “good” PC for running local AI workloads looks like. Microsoft attempted to achieve two things with Copilot+ PC spec:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>push hardware manufacturers towards enabling new AI experiences in Windows</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>use its Windows install base strategically to get AI engineers to run their LLMs locally.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two years on, it’s fair to ask why Copilot+ PCs didn’t really take off. There have been a few roadblocks:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of games: </span></strong><span>Some popular games depend on kernel level anti-cheat functionality that still doesn’t work on ARM</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Price premium: </span></strong><span>Copilot+ PCs are more expensive than the average Windows laptop</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>NPUs didn’t take off yet:</span></strong><span> Most Copilot+ PC functionality has since become available on all Windows 11 PCs with GPUs, so there is no edge to having an NPU.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Battery life improvements seem to be the biggest win for the first generation of Copilot+ PCs, with users reporting over 20 hours of video playback and 15+ hours of regular computer usage.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>NVIDIA collaboration</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft and NVIDIA announced the RTX Spark chip in early June of this year. RTX Spark combines an ARM based 20 core CPU (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/61354a97-281e-4f92-9b86-a8e468c3b690?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Grace CPU</span></a><span>) and NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPU on the same chip. Machines equipped with this hardware have capacity for running and training AI models locally, and NVIDIA claims 1 Petaflop of 4-bit floating point precision.</span></p><div performance. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9a78d584-f8a2-4097-98f5-bc9b0f2db4ec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>NVIDIA</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This time, Microsoft was more than just an OS provider; it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d1bf4be2-1c93-43e2-aa37-1a98783485b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>claims</span></a><span> close collaboration with NVIDIA to ensure Windows works well on the new silicon. With the strong compute capacity, increased battery life, and improved x64 app performance, RTX Spark based machines look like a compelling Windows machine on paper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Still, success is not a given, as we’ve seen with Copilot+ PCs before, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83390f9e-6233-4f9a-91ef-46b69dd673e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>was a bust</span></a><span> in demand terms.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Key questions will again include gaming support, and whether the hardware delivers on its promise; for example, no battery performance numbers have yet been published. Microsoft is betting that developers will like it because models are easy to run locally, while the hardware capability should make it fast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, industry sentiment is different than in 2024 when Copilot+ PCs launched. Nobody seriously talked about local inference back then, whereas today, major players </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59d39f16-27a9-4d81-baef-7209de7cd314?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>are already doing it</span></a><span>, primarily driven by cost concerns. In the local inference demo that Scott Hanselman showed us, we saw that at 40 tokens per second the performance is usable for daily dev work.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Takeaways</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Our sense is that Windows has gone from being the most popular “developer operating system” in the early 2010s, to possibly being the least popular choice to build software on – at least within startups! –, by 2026. Much of this decline seems to come from the Windows team fumbling the ARM transition – which Apple got very right! – deprioritizing power users, and shipping features that upset devs, like the mandatory Microsoft login.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft seems to be frantically trying to win back devs, but is it too late? </span></strong><span>Our sense is that Microsoft is attempting to put its developer division “A-team” on Windows, to add features that could woo devs back to the platform. It’s great to see longtime advocates for devs like Scott Hanselman working for Windows, and smaller experience improvements </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4862ca6c-3638-40f0-b15f-375f271ac06d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shipping</span></a><span> on it, but the question arises as to why Microsoft was content to make the power-user, developer experience worse every year, until recently?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Linux seems to be Microsoft’s strategy to get devs to use Windows more. </span></strong><span>Talking with devs, WSL is the most beloved part of Windows. By making Linux seamless to run on a Windows machine, devs can do most of their work on Linux, while running on hardware that Windows machines support.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the strengths of Windows has always been its expansive hardware partnerships and driver support. Even today, the Windows team is probably the single biggest OS development team in the tech industry, and a good part of this team is dedicated to ensuring broad hardware support. And so devs can buy a beefy Windows machine to play games on, and then just spin up their favorite Linux distribution when it comes to getting work done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Local AI inference is another big bet. </span></strong><span>Our sense is that it’s a matter of “when” and not “if” good enough local AI models will run on laptops. Token costs are an ongoing concern at tech companies, and having decent, fully local coding models run on laptops could be a big win for everyday coding use cases. Microsoft is a company without a frontier model, so has additional incentive to make local inference a reality. We’ll keep our eyes on Microsoft’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6d0e8b1f-91de-4e25-9a71-4f4db1cbaaeb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>7 October event</span></a><span> with NVIDIA, where it’s likely to announce a machine with cutting-edge local AI capabilities.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The “agent-friendly” Windows is an opinionated OS approach, and we appreciate Microsoft having an honest go at it. </span></strong><span>AI agents are here to stay: not just for software engineering, but for general knowledge work. Our sense, from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5fbd9f4f-221c-4370-b5d5-cc3105dc680e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>talking with Ubuntu</span></a><span>, is that the leading Linux distribution is more of a “wait-and-see” approach when it comes to adding potential agentic primitives to the OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Windows team, on the other hand, decided to make agents a new primitive: starting by giving them their own identity within the operating system, adding layers of isolation, and iterating on this approach. We expect Microsoft to change its direction quite a bit in the coming months and years because all this is new, and it’s unlikely that Microsoft – or any other OS maker! – will get the primitives right at the first try.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s encouraging that the Windows team is leaning into open source when it comes to agents: MXC and Microsoft Agent Framework are open source and support other operating systems. And Windows ML leverages ONNX, which is also an open, cross-platform standard.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Are OSes becoming less important, overall, for us developers? </span></strong><span>This is a fair question to ask in closing. More AI coding agents are adding cloud support, and at companies like Ramp and Uber, devs run most of their AI harnesses inside cloud environments. Many apps we use for coordinating and planning development – ticketing, documenting, monitoring, or even oncall – are either web apps, or cross-platform apps that run on all major operating systems: macOS, Windows and Linux alike.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this world, how much does an OS really matter? Our suspicion is that it’s probably far less than before – and it could well be hardware capability, configuration, and cost that become more important in choosing workstations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, competition in the OS space is great for developers. For the first time in a long time, Microsoft seems to be the underdog in the dev OS space for devs, so it will surely compete harder than ever, which should mean users will win. Let’s see if Microsoft’s renewed efforts will be enough to woo more devs back to Windows. Good luck to the Windows team in attempting to pull this off! </span><em><span>Thanks again to everyone at Microsoft who contributed to this article!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>What is your take on using Windows for professional development? Leave a comment below with your observations.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxNjkyNzIyOSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTAwOTc3ODgsImV4cCI6MjEwNTY3Mzc4OCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.ubDHS4OTUHDzA2TFzGmi3V3CUgIdpK9TO4Vq_G28gwg?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. If it detects too early, it cuts the user off in the middle of a thought. If it decides too late, users experience awkward delays. Interruptions face the same challenge. When users start talking over the voice system, a separate mechanism has to stop the audio and clear the buffers. If the interruption detection is too sensitive, spurious interruptions can be triggered from background noise. If detection is too conservative, interruptions take too long and feel sluggish, while short interjections like “yes” and “no” can be entirely missed. Full-duplex Architecture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Full-duplex models are designed so they can both listen and talk simultaneously. The model continuously produces audio tokens. When it should stay silent, it simply produces silent tokens. Similarly, it continuously processes the input audio tokens. When the user is silent, those are just silent tokens. This design removes the turn detector entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To better understand, let’s use an open full-duplex model, Moshi [x], as a reference. Moshi converts audio into discrete tokens, similar to how text is converted to tokens for LLMs. The model processes these tokens as inputs and emits new tokens on a fixed clock, roughly one frame every 80 milliseconds. Silence is simply another token that decodes to silence. So the model just needs to learn the behavior during training and implicitly understand when to listen and when to talk from the training data.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" engineering challenges. First, since the model is always running and predicting the next token, serving is costly. Second, the model needs to respond within milliseconds, so it cannot be too large in capacity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI launched GPT-Live-1 in July 2026, a family of full-duplex voice models. It is designed around the challenges described above. The voice model stays small and fast so it can respond within milliseconds. It also relies on delegation to perform expensive reasoning while the conversation keeps going.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How the GPT-Live System Works</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This section explains how OpenAI managed to build a voice assistant around a full-duplex architecture. We cover the ideas and techniques that make it practical at scale in production.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Separating Talking from Thinking</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Normally, a frontier LLM might reason, search the web, and then respond, which can take several seconds. In voice systems, that translates to a few seconds of silence, which is not ideal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To fix this, OpenAI separates talking from thinking. A voice model handles the conversation with the user. Another capable model performs the necessary reasoning and tool calling for more complex queries. The serving system is also built around this idea. It delegates the request to the capable model when needed, while continuing the conversation with the user.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: Two Serving Paths</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Serving two models is tricky. Audio frames should be sent every few milliseconds, but a delegation can take seconds. So we cannot have a shared process for both. GPT-Live splits the traffic. The live path carries audio only. It moves audio between the client and the voice model as fast as possible. The async path handles anything other than the audio, which can take longer. This way, a slow tool call may delay the async path but not the live path.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to make the live path fast?</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main requirement of the live path is that audio must move between the user and the model on a fixed clock. The model processes frames as input and produces them as output in real time. So the user hears a delay when it occurs. As Zahan explains, whenever a bottleneck makes the system fall behind, it starts producing audible artifacts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To meet this requirement, lots of optimizations are needed. For example, the connection must open quickly, the model must keep up with the incoming stream, and frames must be delivered on time. Here are a few engineering techniques OpenAI adopted to keep the live path fast:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Starting a session in one round trip</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Having cheap continuous inference</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Handing off live conversations between model instances</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Starting a session in one round trip</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When the user taps the voice button, the client must establish a connection before any audio can flow. This requires a few network trips, depending on the underlying protocol. GPT-Live uses WebRTC, which is used in most video calling apps. But a standard WebRTC session takes six steps to establish before a single audio frame can be sent. On a mobile network where one round trip takes 60 milliseconds, setup alone can cost over a third of a second.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: history</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Handing off a live conversation between model instances</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Keeping the conversation loaded on one model instance creates a new problem. Model instances may become unavailable. They need to stop and start with demand or receive updates. They may also fail occasionally. In regular systems, this is easy to handle since we can send the request to another available instance. In GPT-Live, the session is tied to the instance that holds its conversation in GPU memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI created a managed handoff mechanism. The system prepares a replacement instance and loads the full conversation beforehand. Once the new instance is ready to be used, the switch happens, so the conversation can continue without any interruptions. This is also useful when other operations need to happen. For example, when the context needs to be compacted, the shortened conversation is prepared on a replacement instance while the original keeps talking. The switch then happens the same way.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>The Async Path</span></strong></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The async path handles everything that is not audio, like delegations and tool calling. These jobs, by their nature, are large and can take longer to complete. Still, results should come back fast enough that the two models feel like one system. Back to our example session. The user asks who won last night’s game, and the voice model starts a delegation. The voice model can buy a little time by doing things like acknowledging the question or thinking out loud for a moment. But it cannot do anything when an answer takes too long. So everything in the delegation loop, including prompt processing and routing, needs to happen fast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To cut latency, we should first understand what is causing it. Most of the time is spent on reading the request. A model that receives a request has to process the entire prompt (prefill) before producing tokens. In a long conversation, that alone can take a noticeable fraction of a second. OpenAI’s fix is to do this reading before it is needed. When a user starts a conversation, the server creates an inference session with the frontier model and sends the conversation so far. By the time the first delegation happens, the model has already everything it needs to produce tokens.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple normal;"><strong><span>How to Evaluate a Full-duplex Voice System?</span></strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A turn-based speech model can be evaluated one turn at a time by sending a request and scoring the response. But with a full-duplex architecture, there are no turns. There is only one continuous stream of audio. This makes evaluation different.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In full-duplex systems, instead of scoring turns, we can evaluate three parts:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversational behavior</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The health of the stream</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Testing the system on real production traffic</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>1. Conversational behavior</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first question is whether the model behaves well in a conversation. This mostly comes down to timing. The model has to continuously decide if it should stay silent, interrupt, or talk. When the user speaks while the model is talking, it has to decide if this is a real interruption or just background noise. These two decisions are called endpointing and barge-in detection.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Endpointing and barge-in</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To evaluate these behaviors, each decision is scored like a prediction. Did the model detect the end of the turn correctly? Did it recognize a real interruption? The mental model for eval is the same. We collect eval data (natural conversations), have it annotated around the dimensions that we want to measure, run inference on it, and evaluate.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>2. The health of the stream</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second dimension of eval is whether the stream itself is healthy. In most serving systems, this is answered with a percentile target like p95. If the p95 latency is good, 19 out of 20 requests feel fast. This works fine as long as unusually slow cases are kept very low. A normal user only sends a request once in a while, so a slow one is quickly forgotten.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But p95 is not reliable in full-duplex architectures. Given that the model runs continuously, a p95 event happens every 20 inferences, which translates  to several times per minute. Even p99 events show up regularly. So the system has to be engineered around p999. In practice, this means designing for fast recovery, since some slow frames are guaranteed to happen in every session.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>3. Testing the system on real production traffic</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The last layer of evaluation checks whether the system works reliably under real traffic. The technique for finding out safely is called a silent launch. Users keep talking to the old system as usual, while a small percentage of voice sessions are routed to the new system. This kind of silent launch catches problems that are normally hard to find. For example, it can find bottlenecks in unexpected places. In GPT-Live’s silent launch, the team found out that a CPU-side service ran out of capacity before the GPUs did. This is something that is generally hard to learn with ordinary tests.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>What Other Teams Can Learn From GPT-Live</span></strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The broad lesson from OpenAI’s GPT-Live is that building for realtime serving is different and more challenging than traditional serving. For example, in voice systems, users hear the worst frame, so average latency is an insufficient metric to monitor. The tail is more important and deserves more engineering. In addition, capacity planning is different in such systems. When a user is having a conversation, the session is occupied the entire time. So capacity should be measured in concurrent sessions instead of per request.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other lesson is that complexity should be handled inside the model. For example, turn detection used to be a small, separate component, and it was a main source of unnaturalness. Moving that decision into the model behavior, which has the greatest reasoning horsepower, made the conversation more natural and the system simpler. In general, whatever stays outside the model should be kept small and focused on the realtime work. This ensures the system remains simple and maintainable.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>What’s Next</span></strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI believes the next generation is voice driving a computer. In the ChatGPT desktop app, it takes screenshots to see what you are working on, starts long-running tasks, and reports back. Along the way, you can ask for status, answer questions, and redirect it mid-task. Zahan says it feels like science fiction.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 item.title: Same People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Same People

Mike Fisher

“We rate individuals. We compare individuals in calibration. Our promotion rubric counts individual output. Our improvement plans correct individuals. We pay a premium to hire individuals, on the theory that whatever made them good travels with them in a backpack. We produce performance as an organization and then account for it one person at a time.”

#Management PerformanceReviews
item.description: Same People

item.title: The Trendy Leadership Trend That Is Trending
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Trendy Leadership Trend That Is Trending

Jade Rubick

"Leadership is often about trends. Your job is to look at the horizon and identify how things are going to trend: (1) What things are getting better over time? (2) What is getting worse over time? (3) How can you make sure that your organization is getting better in every dimension? Jade shares a simple test to survey your organization."

#Leadership Management
item.description: The Trendy Leadership Trend That Is Trending

item.title: What I Believe About The Future Of Software Development
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
What I Believe About The Future Of Software Development

Thorsten Ball

“To plant my flag, to say that these are things I believed in September 2026, here it is on the blog, non-ephemeral. Some of these predictions are just observations, they’ve long been true at companies like Amp. Others will take some time to play out.”

#Strategy AI IndustryTrends
item.description: What I Believe About The Future Of Software Development

item.title: The Senior Engineer Death Spiral
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Senior Engineer Death Spiral

Sunil Pai

“A friend recently got a new job, a very senior role, very well paid, and pretty different from his previous gig. He was asking me how to do a 60 to 80-hour week, how to do well enough to get promoted, etc. and as we talked, I realised he was feeling a bit of imposter syndrome and really wanted to prove himself. I ended up giving him a bit of a monologue. this is more or less what I told him...”

#Staff+ WellBeing CareerGrowth
item.description: The Senior Engineer Death Spiral

item.title: Trying The Software Factory Pattern
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Trying The Software Factory Pattern

Will Larson

The software factory pattern is looping on a broad goal, and then relying on the harness to drive progress towards that goal. Will describes the first basic version he’s implemented at his company.

#CaseStudy AI Agents
item.description: Trying The Software Factory Pattern

item.title: Back To Coupling And Cohesion
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Back To Coupling And Cohesion

Daniil Bastrich

“In practice, such principles ultimately come down to managing coupling and cohesion in all their forms and at every level of a system. And once we have a good grasp of coupling and cohesion, there is little point in memorizing the alphabet soup of design principles, let alone fetishizing them.”

#CodeQuality Architecture
item.description: Back To Coupling And Cohesion

The model is available to download, the application is quite straightforward, and the machine has plenty of storage. But when the program tries to load the model, it runs out of memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where local AI development becomes a hardware problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Merely downloading a large AI model to our computer doesn’t mean we can actually run that model. These are also known as weights. They influence how input becomes output. During training, these values are adjusted so that the model becomes better at its task. An 8B model contains approximately eight billion parameters or weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These weights are organized into layers. model, the input text is first divided into tokens. These tokens can represent words, parts of words, or even punctuation. The model processes them and produces probabilities for the next token. Once a token is selected and added to the sequence, the generation of text continues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Producing a complete answer is all about repeating this process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A couple of points to keep in mind here are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Using an already trained model is called inference. The model’s weights normally remain unchanged while it answers a question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training requires additional calculations to update those weights, making the process quite demanding. It requires expensive infrastructure.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This difference helps explain why a model trained on expensive infrastructure can sometimes run on an ordinary computer. The main thing we are discussing here is not the training aspects, but the inference part of a model.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Makes it Difficult to Fit the Model on Smaller Hardware</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every parameter or weight occupies memory. A value stored using 16 bits requires two bytes. Following from this, 8 billion parameters require approximately 16 GB for the raw weights alone. Temporary calculations, software overhead, and information retained during generation require additional space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The location of that memory plays a pivotal role. A computer’s RAM is its main working memory. A discrete graphics card has separate memory called VRAM. A desktop with 32 GB of RAM and 8 GB of VRAM doesn’t automatically provide one equally fast memory pool with 40 GB of space. Though computers with unified memory do share memory between processors, they still face capacity limits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A large SSD can hold the model file. However, executing the model requires its data to reach the processor. If we constantly have to retrieve weights from storage, it is much slower than keeping them in working memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Either way, memory capacity is only one of the constraints. Neural networks also perform a large number of multiplications and additions. Though a CPU can execute these operations, a GPU is much more effective at performing many similar numerical operations in parallel. However, a GPU still needs sufficient memory and support for the numerical operations used by the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, even when a model fits in memory, the processor must read its weights and other information quickly enough.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Memory bandwidth measures how much data can move between memory and the processor in a given time. For many workloads involving one user generating text, moving model data becomes a major limit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Text generation and inference also has two stages:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>During prefill, the model processes the supplied prompt, which allows considerable parallel work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>During decoding, it produces output tokens in sequence.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These stages can have different bottlenecks. A model can fit in memory and still respond too slowly to be useful.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Make the Effort to Run Locally?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Local execution can make existing hardware useful for experimentation and reduce dependence on rented computing resources. This can matter for private documents and proprietary source code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Offline availability matters for desktop assistants, remote installations, and products that cannot assume a reliable internet connection. Local execution also gives developers more control over model versions and application behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, local execution is not automatically cheaper for every workload.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hardware, electricity, maintenance, and response speed all matter. Occasional use of a hosted service can be economical, while frequent use may make local hardware more attractive. The comparison depends on the actual application.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at a few techniques that can help run a big model on cheap hardware.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Quantization: Give Each Weight a Smaller Representation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Quantization reduces the precision used to represent numerical values. In a simplified scheme using steps of 0.1, the value 0.73 could be approximated as 0.7. The approximation introduces an error, but that error may be small enough for the application to tolerate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below that shows the process of quantization:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8549de62-4934-425d-a3b4-967bb4ecaf64?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c87a12be-84d6-4876-a699-b494d39b286e_3162x2122.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":977,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":140964,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/216197621?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc87a12be-84d6-4876-a699-b494d39b286e_3162x2122.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}"
