auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The real representation has many more dimensions than a physical map. Individual dimensions also don’t have simple labels such as “hotel,” “flight,” or “reimbursement.” Meaning is represented through patterns across the complete vector.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The trick is that the application embeds the question into the same space as the document chunks. This way, it can compare the question’s vector with stored vectors to identify nearby passages. Also, the query and document embeddings must come from compatible encoders. However, matching vector lengths alone doesn’t make two models compatible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each searchable record also needs a connection to the original text. The vector helps locate a passage, but the LLM needs the words themselves to interpret the rule. Therefore, a record should connect an embedding with a chunk identifier, the passage text, or its location. Also, metadata such as document ID, section, effective date, and version are present. These fields can be stored together or across connected storage systems. Structured identifiers make it possible to retrieve and maintain all chunks belonging to a document.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Close Is Close Enough?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The search system needs a precise definition of “nearby.” This definition comes from a distance or similarity metric, which compares two vectors and assigns a score. There are different metrics around this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cosine similarity compares their directions while ignoring their lengths.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between their endpoints, so vector length can influence the result.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dot product reflects both alignment and length.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Normalization rescales vectors to length one. When both query and document vectors are normalized, dot product equals cosine similarity. Euclidean distance then produces the same ranking, although its scores differ. Dot product also works with unnormalized vectors when that matches the embedding model’s design.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The choice of the metric should follow the embedding model’s intended use. Choosing a metric simply because it is popular can change the ranking in unintended ways.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A similarity score should also be interpreted carefully. A score of 0.85 does not mean that a passage has an 85% probability of answering the question correctly. It describes a mathematical relationship between representations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The passage may discuss the right subject while stating the wrong regional policy. It may be outdated or omit an exception. Similarity provides evidence of relevance, but additional checks are needed before that evidence becomes an answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Searching Every Passage Is Too Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Searching every vector is straightforward, but the work grows with the collection.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A flat index compares the query with every eligible vector and returns those with the best scores. For a fixed number of dimensions, the comparison work grows roughly in proportion to the vector count. This is the meaning of O(n). If the collection doubles, the number of vector comparisons doubles. Longer vectors also require more work per comparison.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Flat search produces exact nearest neighbors under the selected metric. “Exact” describes the numerical search result. It doesn’t guarantee that those neighbors contain the correct answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, an Inverted-File index reduces this work by organizing vectors into groups. During construction, clustering identifies representative centers and assigns vectors to nearby groups. A query can then select promising groups and search their contents. The parameter commonly called nprobe controls how many groups are examined. However, searching more groups generally improves recall but also increases work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Imagine one million passages divided into 1000 groups. Searching 10 groups might involve roughly 10K passages rather than the entire million. Of course, real groups are uneven, and selecting them also has a cost. The main tradeoff is that a useful passage can belong to a group that is skipped by the search. These groups are mathematical neighborhoods, not tidy subject folders. A travel-disruption rule might sit near insurance documents rather than ordinary expense policies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>IVF therefore introduces approximation. It saves work by accepting some risk of missing the nearest vectors.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Following Connections to the Right Neighborhood</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) avoids exhaustive comparisons by building routes between vectors. Its structure is a graph. In other words, points are connected by links.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each point represents a vector. The links provide routes through the collection. HNSW organizes these connections into layers, with sparse upper layers and a detailed bottom layer containing all vectors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, search starts near the top and moves toward points closer to the query. It then descends through the layers, progressively refining the search. At the bottom, it explores a broader set of nearby candidates to select the results.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can think of this navigation like travelling through a road network. Major routes help reach the right area, while local roads help locate a specific destination. HNSW uses this broad-to-detailed pattern to avoid visiting every point.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like the Inverted-File index, it performs approximate nearest-neighbor search. However, selected routes can miss a true nearest neighbor. Its benefit is that useful results can often be found with substantially fewer comparisons.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is no fixed collection size at which flat search must give way to Inverted-File or HNSW. Hardware, vector dimensions, query volume, memory, filtering, and latency requirements all influence the choice. HNSW is a strong candidate when memory permits, but we cannot say that it is automatically the best option for every workload.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A collection searched a few times per day creates a different problem from one serving thousands of simultaneous users. Vector count alone cannot capture that difference.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Much Searching Is Enough?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Approximate search creates a measurable tradeoff between speed and recall.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say an exact search identifies the 10 nearest vectors. An approximate search returns eight of those same vectors and two others. This measures how closely the approximate search reproduces exact nearest-neighbor results. It doesn’t measure whether the returned passages really answer the employee’s question. Both index recall and actual evidence relevance need evaluation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>HNSW has several settings that have an impact on this tradeoff:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>M controls graph connectivity. Higher values generally provide more routes, improving recall while increasing memory use and construction work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>ef_construction controls how broadly the algorithm searches for suitable connections during insertion. A larger value generally produces a better graph but takes longer to build.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>ef_search controls the breadth of candidate exploration during a query. Increasing it generally improves recall while increasing search latency. It isn’t the number of results returned or a fixed count of visited points.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application may need five passages while exploring a much larger candidate set to find them. Result count and search effort are separate decisions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For tuning, we should use representative questions and actual performance measurements. If a broader search consistently finds a previously missed cancellation exception, the added latency may be worthwhile. However, if answers don’t improve, changing the setting merely adds work.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Closest Match Might Be the Wrong Policy</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarity must also be combined with rules about which documents are eligible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, our employee needs the policy for their country and business unit, with an effective date that covers the journey. A highly similar passage from another region cannot help answer their query.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We use metadata filtering to define the eligible subset. The request becomes “find the most similar passages among current policies for this employee’s region.”</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Pre-filtering identifies eligible records before similarity ranking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Post-filtering retrieves similarity candidates first and then removes records that fail the conditions.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If only two of the first 20 candidates qualify, post-filtering cannot supply 5 eligible results from that batch. Retrieving additional candidates may help, but requires more work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nevertheless, pre-filtering is not automatically faster. The outcome depends on how selective the filter is and how the search engine combines filtering with its index. Graph search adds another complication. Disallowed points may still provide useful navigation routes toward allowed points. Blocking every such point during traversal can make eligible neighbors harder to reach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Search engines can address this through filtering-aware graph structures, traversal strategies, or an exact scan when the eligible subset is small. Filtering can therefore be integrated into search rather than occurring entirely before or after it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Happens When the Answer Changes?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The collection must remain correct as its documents change. For example, let’s say the company raises its hotel reimbursement limit from ₹5,000 to ₹7,000. If both versions remain eligible for current-policy searches, the assistant may retrieve either figure or receive contradictory evidence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Changes to embedded text require new embeddings. However, an update doesn’t always require rebuilding every chunk. Unchanged chunks may be reusable, and stable identifiers can support replacing existing records.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A metadata-only change can often be applied without re-embedding, provided that metadata was not a part of the text used to create the vector. Some vector databases can expose separate operations for changing vectors and metadata.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For our policy example, a sensible design can prepare the new version’s chunks, verify their availability, and then change which version is eligible for current searches. Older versions can remain accessible for historical questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That transition requires some sort of coordination. Deleting old chunks first can create a temporary gap. Inserting new chunks first can create temporary duplication. Version identifiers and explicit active-version rules help make the change predictable. Lastly, changing the embedding model requires similar planning but on a much larger scale. Existing documents generally need embeddings in the new model’s space, and queries must use the matching representation.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>From Promising Matches to a Supported Answer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The final retrieval step turns promising matches into evidence the LLM can use. For example, a vector search might return 30 candidate passages. A reranker can compare each passage’s text with the question and select the most useful few.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hybrid search adds another source of candidates by combining semantic retrieval with keyword-based retrieval. Embeddings help connect “cancelled flight” with “travel disruption,” while keyword search can preserve exact matches for policy identifiers, names, or unusual technical terms. Reranking can refine the combined results.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application then supplies the selected text and source details to the LLM. For the stranded employee, this should include the current reimbursement rule, the relevant conditions, and enough context to explain how the policy applies to their situation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The search must also accommodate the scenario of an unanswered question. Every collection has nearest vectors, even when none might contain useful information. Returning the closest passage doesn’t mean that an answer exists. For example, if the retrieved documents discuss ordinary hotel bookings but say nothing about cancellations, the assistant should explain clearly that the available policy details don’t have a clear answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finding a useful passage among thousands of documents requires several parts of an LLM application to work together. Documents first become smaller, meaningful chunks. Embeddings represent those chunks as vectors, allowing the search system to connect a question with passages that express related ideas, even when their wording differs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the collection grows, indexes make that search more efficient. Flat search compares every eligible vector, while IVF and HNSW reduce the work through grouping or graph navigation. These approaches introduce tradeoffs between speed, memory, and recall that need to be measured against real questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarity alone, however, cannot establish whether a passage is suitable evidence. Metadata filters help select the correct region, document type, or policy version. Careful updates keep outdated and duplicate passages from appearing in current searches. Hybrid search and reranking can further improve the evidence selected for the LLM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>The final answer depends on the quality of this entire process. For the employee stranded at the airport, success means finding the current reimbursement rule, preserving its conditions, and explaining it clearly.</span></p></div></div><div underline;">Unsplash</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One morning, my pager went off at 2:14. (This was back when Amazon forced us to have physical pagers like the cool kids in the 90s.) It made a harsh and grating sound that I still remember to this day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A service I owned had stopped accepting traffic. Three downstream teams were also paged. The service had shut down because a certificate had expired at midnight. Renewing it wasn’t difficult; it took about 20 minutes to complete.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What bothered me afterward wasn’t that we had missed it but, rather, </span><em><span>why</span></em><span> we had missed it. The team had spent the previous month in incident mode. Virtually every day there had been fires we had to put out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nobody was ignoring the certificate, or the dozen other small maintenance items like it. It was just that nobody had a free twenty minutes to remember those items existed. We were too busy fighting fires to do the work that prevented fires, and so the fires kept coming.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve seen this pattern everywhere. It shows up in software teams, in our careers, our households, and even our calendars. And once I first began to see it, I couldn’t help noticing it everywhere.</span></p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You’ve probably seen the Eisenhower matrix. Everything you could do gets sorted along two axes, urgent or not, important or not, which gives you four boxes. The bottom row, the unimportant stuff, is easy. You either want to skip it or hand it off.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This article is about the top row, which describes the same work but at two different stages, because that’s where the trouble is.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And the trouble starts when we starve the first half of that top row.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Important and urgent” runs your day, because urgency is the absence of choice. When something is due at five, or a customer is waiting, or the service is down, you don’t decide whether to act. You just act.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Important but not urgent” has the opposite problem. Nothing in it has a deadline. Nothing in it has a person on the other end who will be disappointed if it doesn’t get done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, you’ve been meaning to book a dentist appointment, but it keeps slipping. Now you need an emergency procedure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Maybe you’ve been meaning to call an old friend, and every time you think of it, it’s too late in the evening, or you’re in the middle of something, and you’ll do it tomorrow. Eventually, an important relationship is lost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most explanations of the matrix leave out that the top two boxes are the same pile but at two different stages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything important and urgent was, at some earlier point, important and not urgent. The expired certificate was once a mere maintenance task. But because it was deferred, it turned into a 2am page that woke up four teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason you’re buried in urgent work, and will stay buried, is that the important-but-not-urgent box, the half of the top row of the matrix, is being starved.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cycle goes like this. Urgent things fill your plate. Non-urgent items get skipped. That skipped work turns urgent. Your urgent plate fills again, a little fuller than before. Repeat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The end result? You’re always fighting fires.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You get stuck in this loop by being reasonable. Each time you handle only the thing that’s due today, you’ve made a sensible call. But that approach becomes a problem when that’s what every day turns into.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The only way out is to break the cycle. You have to find a way to do important things before they become urgent.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>What It Looks Like</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Starvation of important work, ironically, looks like a full calendar. Here’s what tends to get left out, and what it turns into.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Updating your resume while you like your job, instead of doing it in a panic after a re-org or layoff.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Writing down your accomplishments as they happen, instead of assembling them from memory a year later.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Telling your manager you want more scope, instead of finding out someone else got the project because they asked first.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Writing down how the system works while you still remember, instead of being the only person who can fix it, forever.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fixing the process everyone works around, instead of waiting for it to break for real.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Going to the dentist regularly, instead of procrastinating until you need a root canal.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prioritizing good sleep, instead of running on five hours and wondering why everything feels harder than it should.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Reaching out to a former colleague now, instead of when you need a favor.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Giving a peer feedback while the problem is small, instead of when it has become a problem with a name.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Checking in on your goals every quarter, instead of realizing in December that you forgot what they were.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Picking up the skill you’ll need in two years, instead of trying to learn it in the two weeks before you need it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Calling your parents, instead of wishing you had.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Writing your will or doing estate planning, instead of leaving it to someone else to decide what your wishes are.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fixing the door that sticks, instead of shoving it for another five years.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>Breaking The Loop</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cycle doesn’t break on its own. You have to break it on purpose.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Trace the fire back.</span></strong><span> After the next emergency, figure out what would have prevented it. Usually it’s something small and boring that never had a deadline. Then look at what’s sitting in your not-urgent-but-important pile right now. Does anything look like it might become urgent in the near future? If so, treat it as part of the cleanup. You’re already in firefighting mode, so extinguish the sparks that could cause the next potential fire while you’re there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Make up a deadline.</span></strong><span> Important things often don’t come with a deadline, so give them one. This is how I finished my book. I had so many fires going that the only way it was going to happen was if I picked a date and treated it like it came from someone else. Parkinson’s law usually works against you: work expands to fill the time you give it. Give it less time, and it will shrink to fit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Finish what you start.</span></strong><span> Here’s a pattern I see all the time. Things calm down for a week, you pick up something important, then halfway through, something urgent shows up, and you drop it. Now you’ve spent the time but gotten nothing. When you pick up a non-urgent thing, commit to finishing it. Extra hours spent on something that prevents the next fire is the best overtime you’ll ever work.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>An Exercise</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Think back to the last three emergencies you had to deal with at work or at home. Next to each one, write down the thing you could have done that would have prevented it or made it a much smaller incident.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now think about whether there’s something similar that you are putting off because there’s no urgency to it at the moment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s your next fire, but it hasn’t started yet. Pick a date, put it on the calendar, and finish it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything important is optional until it isn’t. Do it now while it’s still your choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong>Enjoyed this week’s newsletter? Give it a ❤️ so I know to write similar ones in the future.</strong></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>A Life Engineered will always be a free publication, but if you’d like to support it, we’d be honored if you upgraded your subscription. Emoji', 'Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>It’s rare to work with an unlimited token budget, but at OpenAI, that’s what all engineers, researchers, finance colleagues, and marketing folks do. Recently, I visited one of the world’s leading frontier labs to find out how OpenAI operates today – and for a glimpse at where software engineering might be headed as a profession.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Plenty has changed since I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aed2f1e3-dce2-4bc6-a03b-da581b34f402?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>visited</span></a><span> OpenAI’s headquarters last year. Within a year, Codex has gone from a “nice-to-have” tool to being the backbone of pretty much everything at the company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To learn more, I talked with seven engineering leaders and engineers there: Venkat Venkataramani (VP of Engineering, Applied Infra), Sulman Choudhry (Head of Engineering, ChatGPT), Andrew Ambrosino (Lead, Desktop), Joe Gershenson (Lead, Core Agent team), Akshay Nathan (Engineering Lead, Productivity), Ahmed Ibrahim (Engineer, Codex) and Steve Coffey (Engineer, Responses API). </span><em><span>Thanks to all for taking part!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Codex takes over at OpenAI. </span></strong><span>In a matter of months, nearly all OpenAI’s non-engineers moved over to Codex and ChatGPT Work without a mandate from above for it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Death of the IDE & pull requests. </span></strong><span>IDE usage has been down since January when Codex usage started to surge. PRs and code reviews need to be rethought.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>OpenAI’s agentic software factory. </span></strong><span>OpenAI has built a “software factory” with several automated, agentic feedback loops: for example, Perf Factory monitors production and kicks off Codex agents to automatically fix performance issues.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How engineering tooling & practices are changing. </span></strong><span>Hand-built internal tools are slowly being replaced by Codex, which is increasingly preferred for debugging over specialized tools. Harness efficiency is critical in software factories.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering for a billion users: how OpenAI scales up its infra. </span></strong><span>They buy first and take it in-house later. Also, geographic infra distribution, capacity planning tactics and challenges.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Making OpenAI’s API more reliable and performant</span></strong><span>. CPUs are becoming a bottleneck, doing slower deployments on purpose, and solving load challenges.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How the software engineering job is changing. </span></strong><span>Engineering specializations are disappearing, judgment and agency are more important, and it only takes one or two engineers for previously “impossible” rewrites and migrations to succeed.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Before we start, a scheduling update: I’m in New York for the week, attending the LDX3 conference and visiting a few startups and tech companies in the city,  so there will be no edition of The Pulse on Thursday. Normal service resumes next week!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2fd49ff1-8f59-42c0-ba34-64227a7296d7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>1. Codex takes over at OpenAI</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway from my visit to the company’s headquarters which really sticks out is that Codex – and lately Codex </span><em><span>and</span></em><span> ChatGPT Work – have taken over </span><em><span>everything</span></em><span> there, starting in around January. Desktop lead, Andrew Ambrosino, told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The big theme of the past months has been that everything is now a coding agent. Whether the visible code is your output or not, agents write your artifacts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Think of it like this: your entire life is via software. You have these powerful tools (agents) in your computer, and the ability to loop and reason and write code is the ability to do everything.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The token usage chart below shows this sudden adoption surge:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/86c7b79e-cd31-435e-8048-84223e707601?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Codex usage since August 2025 at OpenAI by department. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7aaac0c5-fa11-4adf-91c3-5a060138d33f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>OpenAI</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a four-month period, non-engineering orgs like finance, recruitment, and legal went from ~0% usage of Codex to 90% usage. Now, almost all OpenAI employees use Codex and ChatGPT Work weekly. So, what happened?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI released the Codex app for Mac in February and for Windows in March, and ChatGPT Work (powered by the Codex harness) in July. Following that, non-engineers there moved all their workflows over to Codex and then to Work.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><em><span>Caveat: OpenAI’s internal version of Codex is a lot more advanced than its external counterpart because it’s plugged into pretty much every OpenAI system</span></em><span> –</span><em><span> similar to how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf4ee2a0-af49-4b0f-9e16-b7de4f3b86f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ramp’s Inspect AI agent</span></a><span> has been wired up.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fascinating part of this is that OpenAI got close to 40% adoption across non-engineering teams at a time when the Codex app was hostile to non-engineering users (hard to use). Between February and April, the Codex app still showed the code on-screen, but even so, non-technical colleagues outside of engineering </span><em><span>still</span></em><span> used it because it could do complex work like researching and creating a presentation, document, spreadsheet, or tasks that produce rich output. Today, those folks are very heavy users of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Being able to work for longer on more complex things drove adoption. </span></strong><span>OpenAI added the /goal setting to Codex, where you can set up a goal for the agent and it keeps working until it is complete. Between April and May, usage surged from 60% to 90%. Andrew believes improvement in the harness’s handling of long-running tasks was one cause of this:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The number one thing that is changing is that people are starting to use threads for much longer, and this longer usage has been a breakthrough. It’s surprising to see the sheer length of time that people spend on a thread – even days! They often set a goal and then have the model crank.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Codex being good at longer-running tasks seems to cause people to do fewer things in parallel. This is because a long-running agent often spins off other agents to do other things, reducing the surface area that you, as a human, have to manage.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Awareness overhang” is another cause of the rapid adoption, the Codex team believes. </span></strong><span>As Akshay Nathan, Engineering Lead, Productivity team, told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“For a long time, we had a ‘capability overhang’: the models were capable but the products didn’t fully bring that out. Now, we’re seeing an awareness gap. Some people have figured out they can use Codex to monitor Slack, update Airtable, or create onboarding materials. But many others still use it for one task and then discover more uses from teammates via word-of-mouth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But there’s still so much more, under the surface, that you can do with Codex.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Role-specific and team-specific plugins are created and distributed. </span></strong><span>Another thing that sped up adoption is that each group started to distribute useful role-specific workflows as plugins. Andrew explained why it’s important to not just offer a generic coding agent:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“If you build a product that can do anything, teams need a way to make it their own. You can’t just give everyone an empty box. Skills and plugins let teams adapt the agent to their work. Sometimes, we also need a new app capability, like a browser that the agent can use alongside those skills. But the same building blocks already cover a lot of different roles.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Subject matter experts are embedded in ChatGPT Work engineering teams. </span></strong><span>The models have become “smarter” than developers in some domains, so devs cannot channel “taste” into the harness in those areas. So, people who are domain experts are onboarded onto engineering teams. This is one outcome of ChatGPT Work being used by so many non-engineering domains: experts embedded with engineering advise developers on things like what a good slide deck, spreadsheet, or business report looks like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Of course, domain experts being in engineering teams is a decades-old best practice for building quality products. It seems like this gets rediscovered in different contexts every few years!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>OpenAI is fully dependent on Codex and Work. </span></strong><span>This is so much the case that in the event of even a minor outage, internal messages from colleagues alert the Codex and Work teams at the same time as – or before – automated alerts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, work happens through Codex and Work, and pretty much </span><em><span>nothing</span></em><span> else. </span><em><span>From the outside, this dependence on a single shared harness is particularly eye-catching; two years ago, there were no AI agents, only advanced AI autocomplete!</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>2. Death of the IDE & pull requests</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Late last year, the Codex team was torn about whether to release the Codex desktop app. Andrew recalls the hesitation:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“In December 2025, we weren’t entirely sure if we would release the Codex app. We had the Codex CLI as a terminal, and there are large, feature-rich IDEs out there. So, would there be space for a dev tool that is between a terminal and an IDE? In my head, there was this future where it would not work out, and be the kind of ‘misfit’ like the iPad was.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A lot of people buy iPads and then never use them: they either use their smaller, more portable smartphone </span><em><span>(which could be the equivalent of the CLI in this metaphor)</span></em><span>, or their feature-rich laptop </span><em><span>(the equivalent of the IDE).</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, don’t forget that in November, Antigravity came out as a VS Code fork. This added to the feeling that perhaps we should have also forked VS Code for the Codex app. But still, we dismissed the temptation and went with our gut feeling that as AI agents get better, IDEs will matter less.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Indeed, since January, IDE usage has gone down and OpenAI’s bet looks like a good one. However, the Codex app is becoming a </span><em><span>little</span></em><span> more akin to an IDE: for example, the ability to edit files inside the app was shipped in June.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>CI/CD systems are seeing massive load increases. </span></strong><span>One sign of productivity gains from Codex is the amount of additional code flowing through OpenAI’s dev infra systems. More code being created and pushed leads to new scaling challenges which the team is currently heads-down on solving. Venkat Venkataramani, VP of Engineering, Applied Infra, said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The number of pull requests (PRs) per engineer is growing like a hockey stick </span><em><span>(at a very high, accelerating rate)</span></em><span>. Every part of the build-test-deploy pipeline is seeing dramatically more load.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re talking about roughly a 10x increase in load on some systems. At most companies, that kind of growth might happen over two or three years. At OpenAI, we see it in about six months.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That level of acceleration exposes bottlenecks everywhere: version control has to handle far more code being written and pushed, CI/CD systems have to scale with it, and production release processes have to absorb a much higher rate of change.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Every month, we wake up to a new set of infrastructure scaling challenges to solve. </span></strong><span>Just when we think we’ve created enough capacity for the next phase of growth, the model unlocks another wave of capabilities, which creates a new set of bottlenecks somewhere else in the system.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In this context, PRs and code reviews are being rethought. </span></strong><span>They have “core primitives” in software engineering, but this level of development acceleration is an opportunity to reimagine them. Again, from Venkat:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The question we ought to ask ourselves in the middle of all this development acceleration is how do we reimagine many things we took for granted. For example, how do we reimagine the CI (continuous integration) and CD (continuous deployment) process? What does observability mean in this world, and how should people interact with pull requests?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you ask me, the way we do code review today makes less and less sense, and the same is true for pull requests.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re now seeing agentic code reviews that look at code changes through a series of different lenses. In the past, it would have been impractical for a cloud infrastructure engineer and a security engineer to review every single code change. With agents, that becomes possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>We can rethink how code is deployed with agents, too.</span></strong><span> We are building an agent that “handholds” a change all the way to production — whether it’s a code change or a change behind a feature flag. It observes the relevant monitoring graphs, but can also build its own dashboard to monitor important signals. More of our code changes are going to production with this kind of agent monitoring.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>An increasingly painful bottleneck is in deploying native mobile apps. </span></strong><span>When there are ten times more pull requests, it’s challenging to deploy on the backend or the web and more infrastructure is needed to do so. Then, after you rework a CI/CD system and make sure there’s enough capacity to run them, you’ll be deploying that many more PRs to production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This arises in the shipping of updates to native iOS and Android apps because every app update needs to go through Apple’s and Google’s manual approval processes which take hours or days to complete.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Talking with Sulman Choudhry, Head of Engineering, ChatGPT, he explained how the app review bottleneck is affecting iteration speed. Sulman used to work at Facebook and remembers how the social media company sped up shipping mobile releases:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Back in the 2010s, Facebook had a pretty important breakthrough in how to ship native mobile code faster. App Store releases went from monthly to bi-weekly to weekly. At the same time, experimentation and feature flags let teams ship code before it was ready to launch, then turn features on remotely when they were.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That model brought a lot more velocity to mobile.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the age of Codex, I think we’re hitting the next version of this problem. Code generation is getting dramatically faster, but getting that code into users’ hands on native mobile is not. For Codex in particular, where usage is heavily mobile-first, that gap is already becoming painful for us and users.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I expect the pressure here to increase quickly. If software can be written in minutes, waiting days or weeks to get it onto a phone starts to look increasingly absurd.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should be aiming for a world where shipping code on native mobile is as fast as shipping on the web. Getting there will probably require some creative rethinking of what we ship, when we ship it, and what can be activated remotely. Today, we’re nowhere close.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>There’s some irony in how shipping a native iOS or Android app has the exact same challenges today as in 2008, when the App Store was launched. In 18 years, not much has changed! Apple still does not officially allow apps to bypass the App Store review process to ship meaningful experience changes.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>3. OpenAI’s agentic software factory</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The idea of a “software factory” is similar to a physical factory where robots and humans produce autos together. In the software context, it is AI agents and humans producing software. Some manufacturing sites are fully automated “dark factories” where illumination isn’t needed because there are no humans. Could the same fully automated process emerge in software engineering? At OpenAI today, there’s a “software factory” running and it’s all built around Codex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s how the “traditional” software development pipeline used to look, compared to what OpenAI’s agentic infra pipeline looks like today, as described by VP of Engineering, Applied Infra, Venkat Venkataramani:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table
