consider an RAG assistant that answers a question using retrieved company documents. The judge may receive:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The original question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The documents supplied to the assistant.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The assistant’s answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The evaluation rubric.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An optional reference answer.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The judge LLM can then assess qualities such as relevance, factual support, completeness, clarity, and compliance with instructions. For reference, a simplified judge prompt might say:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Evaluate the response using only the supplied policy.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Score each category from 1 to 5:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Accuracy:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does every factual claim agree with the policy?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Completeness:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does the response answer every part of the question?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Relevance:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does it remain focused on the customer’s request?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Instruction compliance:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does it avoid making promises not supported by the policy?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Return JSON with the scores, a short explanation, and the exact unsupported claims, if any.</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can store the output from the judge model to compare with previous evaluation runs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This approach is far more flexible than exact matching because the judge can recognize that differently worded responses express the same idea. It can also identify subtle failures such as answering only half of a question or introducing a claim that might not be present in the evidence.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Different Ways a Judge Model Can Evaluate an Answer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are several common methods for judging an answer. Let us look at each of them in detail.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Point-based Scoring</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, the judge model assigns scores such as 1 to 5 for different quality dimensions. This results in numbers that are easier to track over time as we refine the model under testing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main drawback of this approach is that the meaning of a score may be inconsistent. We need to define every score and its rubric properly.  For example, consider the following scores:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>5: Every factual claim is supported by the provided documents.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>4: The main answer is supported, with one insignificant unsupported detail.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>3: The answer is mostly correct but contains a meaningful unsupported claim.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2: Several important claims are unsupported or incorrect.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>1: The central conclusion contradicts the documents.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Pass or Fail Classification</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The judge model can also decide whether an output meets a minimum standard. We can use it for deployment gates, especially when the requirement is crystal clear. For example, “the answer must not contradict policy, expose personal information, or produce invalid instructions.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A pass-or-fail result is simple, but it hides smaller changes. A score can decline from excellent to barely acceptable without crossing the failure boundary.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Pairwise Comparison</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this method, the judge model receives two answers and decides which one is better. For example, it may compare the response from the current production prompt with the response from a proposed prompt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pairwise comparison is often easier than assigning an absolute score. We can decide whether answer A is more useful than answer B more consistently than deciding whether one answer deserves a score of 3 or 4 out of 5.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make this method better, the order of the answers should sometimes be reversed. Judge models can have a position bias and may start favoring whichever response appears first or second.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Error Identification</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead of merely producing a score, the judge model can also identify specific problems.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The judge model can list unsupported claims, unanswered parts of the question, irrelevant sections, or violated instructions. This is quite useful during the development phase because it explains why a score has changed from one value to another.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Human Evaluation and Calibration</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Despite all the advancements in testing, the ultimate test of a model’s ability depends on human evaluation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human evaluation involves people reviewing model outputs using the same rubric. This is why domain experts are really important when the correctness of an answer depends on legal, medical, financial, scientific, or company-specific knowledge.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, since humans are expensive and slow, they cannot inspect every answer. Their best role is often to calibrate things. To make this work, human reviewers rate a representative sample. The results are compared with the ratings of a judge LLM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, let’s say experts mark 100 answers as pass or fail. The same answers are evaluated by the judge model. The exercise reveals how often the judge agrees with the experts, which types of failure it misses, and whether its passing threshold needs adjustment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human reviewers can also disagree with one another. This usually means that the rubric is a little ambiguous or that the task is genuinely subjective. We should, therefore, measure reviewer agreement before treating human scores as a perfect reference point.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human evaluation for LLMs remains highly important for:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Creating and validating the first rubric.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Reviewing high-risk failures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Evaluating new kinds of requests.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Checking whether automated scores reflect real usefulness.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Investigating disagreement between different evaluators.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Periodically auditing the judge for drift.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Evaluation Stack</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Having gone through all the methods of LLM evaluation, we can now look at the overall evaluation stack.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should understand this proposed evaluation stack as a set of complementary layers rather than a strict ladder where one layer replaces another.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>At the bottom are conventional software tests. These are used to verify deterministic components such as permissions, tool schemas, database writes, and calculations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Golden datasets provide repeatable scenarios on which the entire LLM application can be tested.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Automated checks inspect properties that can be measured reliably, including valid JSON, required fields, exact extracted values, citation structure, and latency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LLM judges evaluate qualities that require the model to interpret meaning. We can use it to assess whether an answer is relevant, complete, supported by evidence, and compliant with a detailed rubric.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Human reviewers calibrate the judge and assess cases where the consequences or subjectivity are too great to rely entirely on automation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Production monitoring completes the stack. A test set can never anticipate every real request, so production signals are needed to reveal emerging failures.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should not treat LLM evaluation as a search for a perfect accuracy number. It is a system for building confidence in a model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Golden datasets make critical situations repeatable. Automated metrics quickly check narrow and objective properties. LLM judges assess meaning according to a rubric. Human reviewers calibrate those judges and handle difficult decisions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most reliable question is therefore not simply, “Is the model healthy?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is the idea that across the situations that matter, does the complete application stay accurate, useful, safe, reliable, fast, and affordable? Also, is there enough evidence to detect when that changes?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>This is the real purpose of LLM evaluation.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table item.title: How to name things
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to name things

Koleman Nix

11 minutes by Koleman Nix Koleman says that good naming is one of the most important skills in software, because vague language usually means vague thinking. Names carry meaning for teammates, future readers, and AI tools alike, so choosing them well is an act of empathy. Rather than following rigid rules, good naming means studying the essence of a thing, looking at how nearby concepts relate, and asking how a reader will understand the name in context. A bad name often signals a deeper design problem worth fixing. Revel is hiring. Build the next generation of software for
item.description: How to name things

item.title: A faster way to convert a timestamp
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A faster way to convert a timestamp

Ben Joffe

7 minutes by Ben Joffe Most datetime libraries compute hours, minutes, and seconds using a chain of division steps where each result depends on the previous one, making parallelisation impossible. By reordering the calculations to break this dependency chain, and using fixed-point multiplication tricks instead of division, you can cut the process from around 16 CPU steps down to just two multiplications.
item.description: A faster way to convert a timestamp

item.title: Good APIs age slowly
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Good APIs age slowly

Yusuf Aytas

6 minutes by Yusuf Aytas APIs that look elegant at first often cause the most trouble later. The real test is how an API holds up after different teams use it, requirements shift, and people rely on behavior that was never meant to be a promise. Yusuf points out that most problems come down to boundaries: once something is visible, people build on it, whether you intended that or not. His advice: Expose as little as possible, because adding later is easy, but removing is painful.
item.description: Good APIs age slowly

item.title: A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat

Hadley Wickham

8 minutes by Hadley Wickham Coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor work by giving an AI model tools to read, write, search, and edit files, plus run shell commands. You can build a basic version with just three functions in around 30 lines of code. Adding targeted file editing makes the agent faster and cheaper, since the model only rewrites changed lines rather than entire files. Safety matters too, as path checks and scoped tools prevent the agent from accessing files outside the project.
item.description: A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat

item.title: How well do agents use test and verification techniques?
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How well do agents use test and verification techniques?

about 1 hour by Dan Luu AI coding agents mostly fail to use testing tools and techniques effectively, even when explicitly told to. Telling agents to use property-based testing, formal methods, or TDD changes their surface behavior but rarely changes the underlying quality of tests. Default instructions with no testing guidance outperformed most specific approaches, because specific instructions mostly just caused agents to do useless work inside unfamiliar frameworks. Simple, targeted nudges away from bad defaults worked better than detailed skill documents or named techniques.
item.description: How well do agents use test and verification techniques?

item.title: Less known LINQ methods
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Less known LINQ methods

Ricardo Peres

LINQ has many useful extension methods that developers often overlook. Methods like Chunk, CountBy, and AggregateBy help with grouping and reducing data, while Append, Prepend, and Index simplify common list operations. Others like LeftJoin, FullJoin, and ToLookup handle more complex data relationships. As Ricardo points out, each method has a clear purpose and can replace manual, error-prone code.
item.description: Less known LINQ methods

item.title: Reading a profiler trace without guessing
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Reading a profiler trace without guessing

Bart Wullems

The Azure Monitor Profiler trace explorer has two views of call stack data: a flame graph and a profile tree. Start with the Hot path feature, which jumps straight to the likely bottleneck. The labels on hot nodes tell you what kind of problem you have, such as CPU cost, lock contention, or async waiting, and each points to a different fix. Code Optimizations can analyze profiler traces automatically and surface bottlenecks without you opening a trace at all.
item.description: Reading a profiler trace without guessing

item.title: ASP.NET Core circuit breaker pattern explained
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
ASP.NET Core circuit breaker pattern explained

Yohan Malshika

When one service in your app fails, repeated calls to it can slow everything down and crash your whole system. The circuit breaker pattern fixes this by stopping calls to a failing service before the damage spreads. It works like an electrical circuit breaker, cutting the connection when something goes wrong and retrying later. This keeps your ASP.NET Core app stable even when outside services go down.
item.description: ASP.NET Core circuit breaker pattern explained
